The second thing I did is I'm making the point how you need a little bit of a smile, but not a gigantic
smile.
And then I just talk about not like a TV evangelist that gets a laugh because people have images of
sort of big fake phony TV evangelists with gigantic smiles on their face.
And that gets a laugh every time.
Is it brilliant?
No.
But again, I'm making fun of myself, making fun of something in pop culture.
And it's making an important point about don't smile too big or have a, you know, a fake smile plastered
on your face, just a little bit of an upturn.
So you look more relaxed when you're presenting on video.
Now, the final big lesson here is, again, I'm not naturally that funny.
I'm not this quick wit who's just has everyone at the dinner party rolling on the floor laughing.
But what I do is similar to what great comedians do, which is I listen.
If something got a joke, I use it next time.
So those two elements I just mentioned have gotten laughs for me again and again and again.
So I reuse them when I have new audiences.
I'm not going to say it again to you because you'll have seen it already.
So that's a part of any great comedians technique and a humorous technique and a great storytellers
technique.
Something gets a laugh as a part of a story in the past.
Reuse it again and again and again until it stops getting laughs.

--- You Aren't Jerry Seinfeld ---

The best source of material for funny stories are going to be your own life.
Again, I would caution you against trying to recycle something you saw on a late night talk show or
a comedy special.
If people want to watch Chris Rock or or Jason Alexander or Jerry Seinfeld, they can watch them with
a click of a button on their TV or their computer or YouTube.
They don't need you to recount something.
So your best stories with humor that will get laughs come from your own experiences.
Sometimes it's just a matter of a little distance, thinking about how embarrassing it was and sharing
that with people.
And it will get laughs and help you make the point.

--- Your Comedy Laboratory ---

If you want laughs.
Remember, so much of it is about trial and error experimentation.
It's very hard to actually engineer something you know is guaranteed to get a laugh.
And that's why the greatest the greatest comedians in the world will tell you so much of their success
is simply that they had the patience, the tenacity, the discipline and sort of the the ability to
withstand pain after getting up night after night, sometimes for two years and getting booed off stages.
Getting one laugh in ten minutes or two laughs in 20 minutes.
And it's this painstaking process of figuring out what works, keep it, what doesn't work, throw it
away, doing it again and again and again.
Now, as a storyteller, the standards for you are lower than if you're a standup comedian.
If you're a standup comedian, the audience is sitting there thinking, You better make me laugh every
five seconds or I'm going to get angry and throw rotten vegetables at you.
If you are a business person in a professional setting and telling a story, if you can get just a handful
of laughs throughout 20 minutes, 30 minutes of a presentation, your audience is going to love you.
They're going to think you're far and away the best presenter they've seen all day, maybe all week,
maybe ever.
So that's the good news.
It's just a few little laughs will make your presentation so much better.
But in order to get those, you can use the comedians discipline of trying things, keeping it when
it works, getting rid of it when it doesn't work.

--- Your Worst Moments Are Comedy Gold ---

Easiest way to get a laugh from an audience.
Just tell a story about something really embarrassing that happened to you, might be embarrassing to
you, but it's funny to other people.
I'm not saying human beings are all cruel, but if you see a cartoon character slipping on a banana,
you know nobody's really getting hurt.
And it's not you.
It can still be funny.
So if you're looking for source material, just look at the most embarrassing things that have happened
in your own life.
Make sure that it ties in to a principle, a message that's relevant to your audience.

--- Don't Seem Like You Are Trying Too Hard ---

All righty.
Let me tell you a story.
This is really funny.
You're going to love it.
Rule number one.
When you want to be funny, don't try too hard.
If you seem like you're trying really hard to be funny, then it's generally not funny.
Don't seem like you're trying.
Also, my advice.
You're going to tell a joke.
Tell something funny.
Don't tell anybody you're telling a joke or that you're telling something that you think is funny.
Just tell it.
The second you tell the audience, let me tell you a joke or let me tell you a funny story.
Several things happen, for starters.
You've stopped saying interesting stuff.
You're now talking about the process which no one cares about next.
People's expectations go way up, even if they like you, even if they're on your side.
There's a part of them saying, Well, he says, it's a funny story.
I'll be the judge of that.
Their standards are going to go way up.
So even if it is funny, they're kind of waiting for it and expecting it.
So you've eliminated the element of surprise.
And even if you get a little chuckle, it's kind of like, ah ha ha, okay, you're not going to get
the same impact as if you just said what you're going to say, and it got a laugh.
So my recommendation.
Use humor.
Try to be funny occasionally, even if you want to tell a joke.
But don't ever tell your audience you're trying to be funny or that you're going to tell them a funny
story or that you're going to tell them a joke.
Guess what?
They'll figure it out.
And if they didn't get a laugh, you can just act like you were telling a story that wasn't trying to
be funny because you didn't set the expectations up in the first place.

--- Avoiding the Hack ---

Don't tell a joke just to tell a joke.
That's what hack comedians do.
That's what bad speakers do because they think, Oh, if I get him to laugh, I'll be more relaxed.
If you want to be a compelling storyteller, everything needs to be done by design.
On purpose, you need to be making a point.
Now, if something's spontaneous, if someone's cell phone goes off and you make a joke about tell the
bill collectors you're not here.
If you want to do something, that's okay.
But you don't want to seem like you've prepared and packaged and you're now going to deliver this set
joke.
You're not a professional comedian now.
Professional comedians can do this because they spent thousands of hours in front of people, often
open mics, practicing their craft.
You don't have time for that.
So you don't have the professionalism, I'm assuming, of a professional comic.
You also don't want to seem like a bad amateur hack comic.
So that's why my advice is don't tell jokes, don't tell a reworn reused, used up joke story that people
have heard.
Just tell your story and if you can bring in personal elements, anything embarrassing to you, any
surprises, then your humor will come across as genuine, authentic, real and not like a stand up comedy
wannabe.

--- Showing the Fun ---

If you want to be funny, you need to convey that something is funny with your face, with your voice,
every part of your body.
Very few people can be like Steven Wright, the famous comedian who has the droll monotone one liners
for the rest of us, if we want people to know something is funny, we have to convey that with our
facial expressions, with our tone of voice, with an actual laugh.
Don't be afraid to laugh if something makes you laugh, too.
This will all send signals to the audience that, hey, you're having fun.
They might as well to.

--- Your Humorous Voice ---

When you're telling stories, it's especially important if you want to be funny to use your voice to
full effect.
We have a whole section earlier on Voices, but if you're trying to bring in humor, you really need
to use your voice for maximum effect.
If you're talking about a character who is clearly a different age, ethnicity, different country from
you, different perspective, different accent, then try to be close to them.
Now, you don't want to sound like you're doing racial stereotypes and offending anyone, but if you
are, for example, a young woman and you are talking about an experience where you had this gruff old
man chastising, you then become a gruff old man with your voice, No one's going to be offended by
that.
Use your voice to convey the character of this person.
And it's okay to exaggerate slightly.
No one's judging you on the standards of are you a professional mimic or a professional impressionist,
But just bringing to life that voice with a slightly exaggerated tone will make the whole thing funnier.
Not every time, but some of the time.

--- The Funny Self-Talker ---

When you're using humor in your stories, don't forget to tell people what you were thinking.
You can bring in self-talk.
Sometimes that can make it funnier.
So much of humor, comedy, you hear this all the time is about timing.
What is timing?
Well, it's really about pausing, not racing.
Too many people when they're giving presentations or telling stories are just racing along.
They're reading as if they were reading a piece of paper and they're reading in their own mind.
And boom, boom, boom, boom.
The mind can't catch up with it.
So you need to give people space to connect the dots, to visualize this embarrassing thing that just
happened to you, to answer in their own mind what they would be thinking.
So when people talk about timing, it's quite often just pausing more and not racing.
So you've got to really factor that in.
If you tell a story and you give people time to think about it, quite often they'll come to their own
conclusion that it was in fact funny.

--- The Bottom Line on Humor ---

Final thing to think about when it comes to adding humor in your storytelling is you can dissect it.
Chop it, slice it and dice it all day long.
At some point, people either find it funny or they don't.
You don't have to be wildly funny to be a good storyteller, but the more humor you have generally,
the more people will like you, the more they will remember you, the more your other messages go down.
So it does behoove you to try to think about how can you add elements of humor in your presentation?
Bottom line is, if it works, it works.
Keep using it.
If it doesn't work, it doesn't work.
And this the ultimate authority is not me.
It's not any other public speaking coach or humor coach.
The ultimate authority is your audience.

--- Your Humorous Story ---

I haven't asked a lot of you in this course so far.
It's time to bring out your cell phone, your webcam, and let's just practice trying to be humorous,
having a story with a humorous element.
And all I want you to do is to retell something embarrassing that happened to you or something awkward
and how you reacted to it.
Try to bring in all the story elements from before and try to do something where we can visualize this
embarrassing thing.
If you want to try something else to bring in humor or have some fun, that's fine too.
But practice this speech right now.
Do it as many times as it takes until you like it and then upload it to YouTube, Facebook, Google
Drive, put the URL right here and the Q and A section and let us watch it.
Let's all have some fun.

--- Don't Do This ---

In this section, I'm going to cover common blunders people make when they're telling stories or they're
planning stories.
I don't like to lead with mistakes to avoid because I find it's much more productive to help people
focus on what does work.
But there is a place for talking about blunders and mistakes, and here it is.
So take a look.

--- The Biggest Blunder of All ---

By far the biggest mistake people have regarding storytelling is simply not having a story that is far
and away the number one mistake.
People in business, politics, culture, civic life is they just don't have stories.
They try to tell people at the abstract level, the fact based level they do a data dump.
Nothing is remembered.
The whole speech, the whole presentation was a complete waste of time because it was instantly forgotten.
Now, I hope you're not even tempted to make this mistake after being in this course this long, but
realize it's always easy to slide back into the old habits.
And the old habits in most organizations is you've got a presentation, it's on the calendar.
Someone in the PowerPoint department will start coming up with slides.
The slides go back and forth legal.
And before you know it, all this time has been spent creating this this deck, this presentation,
and it feels like it's this old monster that you can't even control anymore at that point.
Oh, my gosh, it's too late to put in stories, right?
Wrong.
It's never too late to put in storage.
But ideally, don't let it get to that point.
That's not how your presentation should be created.
Your presentation should be created with you asking yourself, What do you want the audience to do?
What messages are going to do that?
And then what stories do you have for each one?

--- Don't Cut That ---

Next biggest blunder people make regarding stories.
Less time than they thought they had got to cut something.
Let me cut out the stories because there's so much important data to go through.
Big, big mistake.
If you thought you had 20 minutes and you had three points and three stories and now someone tells you
you've only got ten minutes, don't cut out your stories.
Cut out some of those data points, those extra facts, those extra slides.
Stick with your stories, because that's what people will remember.
They're not going to remember the bullet points, the numbers, the little chart lines that go like
this.
That's not what they're going to remember.
So don't delete the stories.
Delete extra data.
Keep your stories, especially if you have less time than originally scheduled.

--- Should Be Obvious, But Is Not ---

Another big blunder people make is telling a story that some in the audience interpret as racist, sexist.
Off color offensive to certain minority groups or religious groups or sexual orientation groups.
And no, you can't get away with it by saying, well, I was just quoting someone else or I was just
passing along with someone else.
No, it's going to stick to you.
So you have to be very concerned about, again, your audience, how are they going to interpret it?
The fact that you like it and it's harmless to you doesn't matter if people in your audience are offended.
Because if people are offended by your story, that's what they're going to remember that you're an
offensive person, not the message that was supposed to be helpful to them.
So that's the real problem with racist, sexist, offensive jokes and stories is it's not about being
politically correct.
They're just not effective.
They don't help you communicate because they're distracting people and they're just making people not
like you.
So that's a big blunder people continue to make.
Don't practice your stories and don't test your stories on people who look 100% like you and sound like
you and are the same age and the same ethnicity as you.
You should practice.
You should have some circle of people that really represent your audience, and that way you can get
some feedback.
If something is bothering people, I remember once, many years ago it wasn't in a story, but it was
in a PowerPoint presentation.
I was stressing to people that when you're doing a media interview, you need to have your eyes staring
at your message points, not looking around the room or staring at Facebook or your website.
But you should literally be staring at your message points to increase the odds that the message points
come out of your mouth when doing your interview.
So I had an image.
It was an image of a person whose eyes were bulging out.
I thought it was a little bit funny.
More important, I thought it really drove home the point.
Keep your eyes on your messages so it didn't have a slide with a whole bunch of text.
It wasn't confusing.
It wasn't trying to convey too many ideas.
It was one idea.
So I was following everything I thought was a best practice when it comes to using PowerPoint.
But one day.
One of my audience members came up to me afterwards and said, TJ, that slide I personally find racist.
I find it offensive.
Had not occurred to me, to be totally honest.
But I listened carefully.
I was a little annoyed at first, but then I realized, you know what?
This person just did me a huge favor because if he finds this slide annoying, racist, offensive,
guess what?
Maybe there are a lot of other people do, too.
And you know what I did with that slide?
Boop.
I hit delete and I just came up with a completely different image.
So that's what you need to be on the lookout for when it comes to your your presentations with your
stories in them is it's not about being overtly racist and using the N word.
Obviously.
I'm assuming you're not going to do that.
But sometimes it's just an image.
Sometimes it's just one cultural reference in your story that some people could find offputting or offensive.
You need to listen, you need to respond, you need to edit.
Sometimes you need to delete.

--- Less Is Not Always More ---

Another common blunder being too short.
There was this time I gave a speech and the introduction was a little too long, so I made mine short
and I got off the stage.
Well, guess what?
That's not a story.
I said that in about 10s, but there's not enough there.
You don't have a sense of the characters, the setting, the problem, the nothing.
So that's a huge problem for a lot of people.
They think they're adding stories, but they're only talking for 10s and they're just giving a couple
of elements.
People come to me all the time say, TJ, teach me to be concise.
I want to be concise.
They stand up, they speak, and their whole speech is two minutes and they try to cover.
Nine points.
They don't have a single story, a single really interesting example.
And they sit down.
Well, they were concise.
And then I asked people, what does anyone remember from what this speaker just said?
Nothing.
So.
I want to change your thinking.
I don't think your goal should ever be to be concise.
Now, you don't want to go on and on and on and have too many words and drown out your message.
But your goal isn't to be concise.
Your goal is to communicate your messages.
Your goal is to be memorable.
When telling a story, it's to tell people as much information as they need to really have an investment
in the characters.
The problem, the solution, the conflict, the emotion and what the message was.
You don't have to talk for ten minutes.
You don't even have to talk for three minutes for a story.
But you're going to have to talk longer than 10s.
So avoid this common blunder of just being way too short and too concise.

--- More Is Sometimes Less ---

Another common blunder people make is being too long.
They're going on and on and on.
Maybe it started off interesting, but the audience is thinking, Where's TJ going with this?
I'm not saying it.
It's getting late.
I've got email to check.
If people don't know why you're going in a certain direction, if they're just seems like there's too
much detail or you're going off on tangents, that's a huge problem.
Your storytelling will not be effective.
So sometimes you want to talk it out, look at it and try to edit it down, Try to figure out what can
I cut out of this and still keep the meat, still keep the good stuff.
So it can be a problem of going on too long.
In my experience, the far more common problems people not having stories or being too short.
Remember when the movie came out?
The Titanic?
It was the most successful movie in the history of movies, and it was three hours and 15 minutes long.
Now, they could have done the whole thing in a half an hour and just left out a lot of detail.
But would that have been as good a story?
Now, your speech doesn't have to have a three hour and 15 minute story inside.
But just remember, if it's good, people will listen for a long time if it's boring.
Even 30s is too long.

--- Let's Take Things Up a Notch ---

In this section, I'm going to cover a lot of advanced tips on storytelling.
A word of note this is not a completely linear thing where the first lecture leads to the second, to
the third, to the fourth.
So it's not as consistent a whole of a segment as some of the others.
Keep that in mind.
What that does mean is you can jump around, you can click on just the ones that look of interest to
you, but these are meant as standalone tips to help you become an even more effective storyteller.
Enjoy.

--- The Best Written Stories Are Often Not Written At All ---

This is going to be a shock for some of you.
Some of the best public speakers in the world, the best storytellers in the world don't write out their
stories.
They don't write out their whole speeches.
They're good speakers, not because they stay up till 2 a.m. writing and rewriting and rehearsing and
practicing.
No, that's not their technique.
They create a database of stories, and when they're preparing for a presentation, a speech, they
think of it almost like going to a jukebox.
I'll take A three, B, two, C, seven.
They're combining stories with messages.
The order may be completely different, but they look at their presentation in terms of here are the
ideas I'm trying to communicate.
Now let me go into my database to pick the best stories to make those messages come alive.
This is a system that frankly saves a lot of time and makes the whole presentation come across so much
more effective because you will essentially have rehearsed your presentation before because you have
given the stories before.
Obviously, this doesn't work if you're speaking to the same group of employees or the same group of
people again and again.
But if you have similar messages, but you're talking to different groups, this is an extraordinarily
effective way of preparing for presentations.
So put away the pen and the keyboard.

--- Read Your Audience ---

To be a great storyteller.
You have to read your audience at all times when delivering your stories.
Are they crying?
Are they laughing?
Do they look confused?
Are they typing email?
You're trying to figure out what's working, what isn't working?
Are you having the intended effect on your audience or are you confusing them?
What works with one audience might not work with another.
With some audiences, you may need more detail, more repetition.
There's something about live performance, whether it's the theater singing or yes, just giving a speech
or presentation that makes it better.
And that is you can react to your audience, you can read your audience.
You're not just up there like a video projector where someone hit on and you're just going through the
motions.
That's not what any great speaker does.
If you're going to be a master storyteller, you've got to be comfortable enough with your material
and your stories to really be present with your audience, to look at them, to listen to them, to
figure out what effect are you having on them.

--- Make Your Audience a Part of Your Story ---

When you're telling a story to your audience, you can occasionally ask questions of your audience.
It doesn't have to be as simple as yes or no.
Or has that ever happened to you?
Although you could put those in.
What you'll find, though, is in most cases, all the answers to a particular question you have will
come down to 3 or 4 of the basic same answers again and again and again.
So if this is an important point to you and it's a good story, you can ask questions and then you're
ready to react with 3 or 4 different templates.
The beauty of this is your audience doesn't know you've heard the question or their answers before.
They don't know that you've planned this in advance and you're giving off the sense that this is live.
You're thinking on your feet.
This is a conversation.
It's not just a performance, a set thing that's being tossed out.
So get ready to ask questions of your audience, but be prepared for any answer.
Again, you do it often enough and you'll find you'll already know the answers most of the time.

--- Tell Me Something New ---

Whether they realize it or not.
Many in your audience are asking themselves this question.
Does this speaker have a story I haven't heard before?
Do you have a good answer for them?
The rap on a lot of speakers, especially in the motivational genre, is that they're just saying the
same old thing.
They've got a different version of the same old story of, Oh, I was so down and out and I worked my
way up with nothing.
And so you're going to have no problem because you're better off than I was.
It is true.
There are a lot of motivational speakers who follow that basic template.
Now, this can still work depending on how gifted a storyteller you are and how compelling your story
is.
But here's something that will be even more effective and is frankly easier.
Have not only a unique story, but have a unique point.
Deliver an idea that gets people thinking, Hmm, I never really thought of that before.
Do that and you'll stand out.

--- Complexity Makes Your Characters More Interesting ---

When you're describing the characters in your story, bring about some complexity.
If it's just a stick figure, if it's just he's pure evil and he beats children for fun and starves
cats.
It's harder for the audience to relate to that because life is complex and there's good and bad in everyone.
So if you take the time to describe flaws as well as good aspects of the different characters, yourself
included, it's going to come across as more authentic, more believable, especially when you're talking
about yourself.
And ultimately you did something well and something you think people can learn from.
Take the time to physically describe your weaknesses, and any that's less than ideal will make you
sound more believable and more relevant.

--- Share the Pain ---

Are you sharing the pain of your characters now?
Don't make up anything, as I've talked about before in this course.
The best stories are simply real experience you have with real people.
But don't hold back on the pain as you'll see later on when I share it with you more of my stories.
I talk about the pain of just fear of being shot when a talk show host pulls a gun on me.
I talk about the nervousness of giving my very first speech in life.
Don't forget to tell people the pain that certainly you feel, but also that the other characters in
your stories are feeling.

--- The Story Image Lives On ---

When you're telling a great story, remember this the image people put in their own mind as you tell
the story, that's what they'll remember more so than your words, more so than your message.
Sometimes that's why it's so important to test.
Sometimes you can create imagery that's so powerful it can overwhelm your message and your story.
So remember, it's the images people remember often more important than your message to them.
You've got to bring it together.
You've got to make sure there's congruence.
So the image remembered is totally consistent with the message you want your audience to remember.

--- Where Is This Going ---

Remember, unless you're a professional comedian or humorist, it's not enough to simply tell a story.
Your audience needs to know right from the beginning, Where is this going?
What's the point of this?
You need to make sure your audience understands the point.
Otherwise, even if there are some amusing anecdotes, it might leave them scratching their heads.
Why is he telling me this?
Why is she saying this?
There are different standards for you being up on stage or in a boardroom giving a presentation versus
just telling an interesting story about what happened earlier today at the dinner table with family
or friends.
So the standards are higher when it comes to giving official, formal or important business presentations
and stories, on the other hand.
Standards are actually lower because people are not expecting you to have interesting stories.
They're most likely expecting a boring data dump.
So you can win just by delivering a story that has a clear point.

--- Here Is The Best Way to Thank People ---

You've heard me mention that when you're starting a presentation, the easiest, the best thing is to
just start right away into a story.
Start with a setting or introduce the character.
People say to me, T.J., you know, I just can't do it.
It feels weird.
It feels rude, it feels obnoxious.
Of course, I have to thank the organization that invited me.
Of course, I have to thank the person who introduced me, thank people for listening, thank them for
their time.
You could, but you do not have to.
It's frankly boring.
Everyone is expecting you to do that.
Nobody's walking away saying, Wow, awful, boring speech, but I sure am glad he thanked me.
That's not what goes on in the mind of the audience.
I want you to think of it from a slightly different perspective.
I would submit to you that the single best way of thanking the audience, the best way of thanking the
people who who invited you, the best way of thanking the organization.
Is to deliver a great speech, a great presentation filled with great stories.
Do that.
Do it from the beginning and they will feel like you really are thanking them because you prepared your
very best.

--- A New Twist on An Old Story ---

You've heard me mention that the best stories are personal to you, but they don't have to be personal.
But if you're not going to use personal stories, at least tell an old story that maybe people have
heard before, but do it in a new way.
There's got to be a new lesson there, a new twist.
Malcolm Gladwell, the New Yorker writer and bestselling author, does this so well with his speech
on David and Goliath.
He talks about an old story people have heard of for thousands of years, but he tells it in a completely
different way with different lessons.
That's what makes it so effective.

--- Abstraction Is Your Enemy ---

Abstraction is the enemy of great speakers everywhere.
What do I mean by abstraction?
They the company.
We.
It happened.
Be specific.
That's the beauty of telling stories.
It's virtually impossible.
Indeed, it is completely impossible to be abstract.
If you tell a story with all the story elements as outlined in this course.
When you talk about one real person with one real problem and one real place that takes the abstract
concept and allows people to visualize it.
Don't talk about pain with suffer.
Talk about my throat.
My my tooth was throbbing and I was in tears.
I was in so much pain.
That's specific.
Pain is an abstraction.
I call the company.
That's an abstraction.
I called Jim Smithers, the vice president of sales.
And I said, Hey, Jim, I got a real problem that's specific.
So it's okay to introduce abstractions in your presentation.
Intelligent people have to deal with abstract thought, but if you want people to not only understand
it, but remember it, process it and act upon it, you must bring the abstraction down to the concrete
level.
That's what stories are so good for.

--- Show N Tell, Not Just Tell ---

Remember when you were a kid in school?
It wasn't called Tell.
It was called Show and Tell.
Any time you can show something when giving a presentation and telling a story, all the better.
Now, if you have a prop, great.
If you're talking about how you search the world over for that perfect gemstone or that perfect bracelet,
and now you have it, then show it by all means.
But it doesn't have to be a physical object.
If you want to talk about how you're talking to a small child, get down and bend down really low.
If you're speaking to someone who's scaring you a big, scary giant, then make yourself a big, scary
giant.
You don't have to go to acting school.
You don't have to hire Meryl Streep, but use your body to show it.
If you're running away from someone because you're being attacked by bandits, then run at least three
feet across the stage or across the room where you're speaking.
The more you show, instead of just having your lips move, the more memorable you'll be, the more
compelling and the greater impact you'll have on your audience.

--- All Five Senses ---

The best stories use all five senses.
You want to make your audience see where you were.
You want to make them feel what you were feeling.
If something's hot or painful, let them know if there's a sickly sweet smell or there's a fire.
Smell it.
Let your audience really feel like they're experiencing it.
Smelling it.
Are you touching something that's bumpy, harsh?
Is it cold metal because it's a gun next to your neck?
Now, don't make up stuff.
Don't feel like you have to be as overly dramatic as a gun.
It could be.
You're simply sitting at your boring desk job and you're feeling how cold the desk is.
But let people feel it.
How does it feel?
How does it taste?
How does it smell?
How does it sound?
We need to hear the difference in the voices of the characters in your story.
Use all five senses and you'll be much more powerful in your stories with your audience.

--- Increase the Tension ---

Great stories have not just tension between the main characters, but they have increasing levels of
tension.
I understand you can't do that all of the time, but when you can add extra elements of tension, so
much the better.
You thought that you were going to lose a $50,000 client.
Now it turns out something so bad has happened.
You're fearful of losing your whole career at extra elements of tension in your story and you'll bring
the audience along with you.
It'll make for an even stronger emotional impact on them.

--- Think Like a Movie Director, Not a Typist ---

Really great storytellers start to develop the mindset almost of being like a movie director.
You're thinking visually, this scene leads to this scene, leads to this scene.
You're not just thinking about words out of people's mouths.
You're thinking in terms of scenes.
It works for Steven Spielberg.
It works for the top directors in the world.
It can work for you when telling your stories.

--- Be Active, Not Passive ---

The more you can speak in the active voice and in first person, the better.
Leave the passive stuff for others, it's generally not good for writing.
It's certainly not good for storytelling.
Talk about it as if you were there right now.
Talk about yourself.
Use the first person.
Use I use me.
Say what he did.
What she did back to you.
Don't make this overly formalistic, overly complicated.
You will lose your audience if you do this.
Your stories will have much more immediacy.
Be easier to follow and will seem less stilted.

--- Just Tell the Story Already ---

Never tell people you're going to tell them a story.
They'll figure it out.
You heard me mention this earlier, but I just wanted to stress this again for the advanced tip section.
Give your audience a little credit.
They will figure out you're telling a story and use every second of your time for maximum impact.
Telling people you're going to tell them a story is an interesting.
They'll figure it out.
You don't see the director of a Hollywood blockbuster come out at the beginning of the show and say,
Today, I want to show you a movie.
Well, no, we know it's a movie.
We're seeing it right now.
Don't waste time on the obvious.
Instead, spend your time giving compelling details for your story to bring people in.

--- No, You Don't Want to Be Concise ---

I said this earlier and I want to say it again because it's such an important point.
Your goal when you're speaking or when you're telling a story is not to be concise.
I know some of you think that's the goal.
And I have clients come to me all the time say, TJ, teach me to be concise.
No, I don't want you to be long winded just for the sake of being long winded.
I don't want you to speak for seven hours as Fidel Castro once did.
I want you to speak primarily for impact on your audience and take as much time as you need.
It's certainly possible to be too long, but it's far more possible to be too short by leaving out critical
story elements.
So remember, you're not trying to be concise.
You're trying to communicate.

--- Want People Say They Want Is Not Necessarily What They Want ---

If you ask people what sort of a communicator do they want?
What sort of a speaker they want?
They will tell you, oh, we want someone direct.
We don't want someone coming here telling us a bunch of war stories.
We want someone to just give us the meat, give us the substance, be as direct as possible.
Yeah, well, I hear that.
I don't believe it.
Now, if you look at polls, polls will also tell you that voters hate any candidate who uses negative
ads will vote against candidates using negative ads.
And yet the candidate who uses the most negative ads often wins in political campaigns.
And my apologies to those of you in countries outside the US.
I realize that's mostly a US reference because so many countries don't allow paid political TV ads.
My point is what people say they want and what they want are often different things.
I can say I want to lose £30 and eat nothing but fresh fruit and vegetables.
And yet you might catch me later eating an ice cream bar.
Why is that?
It's because you can't always listen to what people say.
You have to listen to what actually works on them and what what they do.
And that's the issue with stories is it's not direct.
Telling a story is less direct than just telling somebody what to do or telling somebody what the point
is.
The beauty of it is it's effective because it's not direct.
It allows people to visualize your point.
It allows them to think about it and quite often allows them to think that the idea from your story
is actually their own idea.
That is the beauty of stories.
That is the beauty of indirect communication.

--- Order Matters ---

Sequencing is critically important when telling stories like this.
If you're baking a cake and you're following a recipe, it wouldn't taste very good.
If you turn the oven on long after you have put all the ingredients in the oven and pulled it out.
There's certain things that have to be done at certain times, otherwise you're not going to bake a
cake.
It's exactly the same thing with a story if you don't introduce the characters first.
Tell us what the problem is.
We're not going to care about the conflict or the dialogue or the resolution or the or the principle
to be learned from the story.
So you have to have the sequencing laid out so that it makes sense.
This is where it's good to practice on video, test, test on others.
Are they following you?
Sometimes you can get so close to a story you can leave out important details.
It still makes sense to you.
Doesn't make sense to anyone else.

--- Make Your Hero Relatable ---

Your chief character in your story needs to be a hero at some level to your audience.
Your audience needs to be able to relate to your hero, relate to the primary character in your story.
But you've got to be careful about this.
Sometimes you can make yourself the hero of the story.
If you reveal enough about your weaknesses, your flaws, and you don't make it sound like you're trying
to be perfect and you're Superman or Superwoman.
But most of the time when you're telling stories, someone else needs to be the hero.
And that way the audience can look up to that person.
They're not always looking up to you.
It'll be much more effective than just talking about yourself.

--- Stories Make Advice Less Annoying ---

Another huge advantage of telling stories.
When you're giving people advice, a story makes the advice go down easier.
It doesn't seem as ham fisted, doesn't seem like you're the dictator just telling them what to do.
That's why parents often like to tell stories to their children.
It's not as annoying to the audience as you're saying.
Do what I tell you.
So if you have customers, clients, prospects, employees, I'm not suggesting you treat them like
children or you think of them as children, but by telling a story, the advice is going to go down
so much easier.
Rather than telling someone, Hey, what you're doing is stupid, it's really going to destroy your
career.
You can talk about someone else, you know, who was in a similar situation, what their problem was,
how they resolved it, and why this was a big issue.
Let the first person be able to relate to it.
Mm That's a little bit similar to me.
Much more effective than just straightforward giving people advice.

--- Leave People Feeling Up About Something ---

Your stories most of the time.
Not all the time, but most of the time need to have a happy ending.
If you want people to be receptive to you, your ideas, whatever it is you're advocating or selling
or trying to persuade them on, they need to feel up after hearing you.
Now you may be talking about some critical problem, a crisis, a tragedy of sorts, but there needs
to be a positive aspect of what can happen or did happen over here and how you intend to duplicate it
over here.
Just if they support you or vote for you or give you money.
So I don't want to suggest that it's impossible to ever talk about negatives or problems, but certainly
the first story you tell in a presentation, the last story, the there needs to be some kind of positive
ending from the story, some positive message that sticks with people, that makes them feel good about
what it is you are trying to do, even if what you're trying to do involves horrible tragedy.

--- The Motivation of Your Hero ---

What motivates the hero in your story and does your hero have some reluctance?
Now, again, when I say hero, I just mean the main person.
And it could be you in your story who does something that people can relate to and see.
This ended up being positive.
It doesn't mean they have to slay dragons or rescue men or women in distress, but there's got to be
some nuance there if you really want to be effective.
Do they have nagging doubts?
Are they being pushed into something that isn't a natural fit with their skills and their interest?
Share this with your audience and your hero will be more interesting, more credible, and more believable
to your audience.

If you ever talked to a lot of great writers, the one thing you'll find in common, they pretty much

This idea here with a little twist or wrinkle can work in something they're writing.

--- How Long Should a Story Be ---

How long should a story be?
The answer is really as long as it takes.
Most people make two mistakes.
They either put in way too many details that confuse people or they're too brief and they don't bring
in actual dialogue and describe their characters in detail.
If you're going on for ten minutes, chances are that's too long.
If you finished your story in 15 seconds, chances are you don't really have all the elements of the
story.
Focus first and foremost on Have you really explained what happened?
Have you introduced characters?
Have you established the problem?
Have you recounted the conversation?
The dialogue?
Have you talked about how you felt the characters felt?
Did you resolve some problem?
And is there a lesson from this?
Focus on that and the time will typically take care of itself.

--- What Is the Best Way to Start a Story ---

What's the best way to start a story?
Just dive right in.
Don't say Let me tell you a story.
Don't tell me out today.
I want to talk about blah, blah, blah.
Just hop in.
You don't have to say thank you.
Good morning or any of that.
Just hop right in to the story.
Establish the setting that is the best way for many reasons.
It's not how most speakers start, although the good ones do, and it's devoid of all the throat clearing
cliches most people use when they start a presentation.

--- Can You Make Up a Story ---

Can you make up a story?
You could, but chances are that's just much harder to do than telling a real story about a real conversation
you had with a real person about a real problem.
So I don't recommend making up stories that's different from retelling a story that you've heard from
a third party or someone else told you about it.
But just to make up something about a fictitious client having a fictitious conversation, that's going
to be harder for you to say.
And remember, it's also going to be harder for your audience because chances are you're going to leave
things out.
So I don't recommend making up stories.
Now, can you blend together a couple of different scenarios and stories and a couple of different clients
and make it a composite?
Yeah, you can do that, but more often it's easier to just focus on one real person, one real story.

--- Should You Memorize a Story ---

Should you memorize your story?
This is a little bit complicated.
Certainly, if you are a world renowned, famed keynote speaker and you're all about the power of your
story and bringing people to tears, at that point, it becomes almost like a Broadway performance.
Speakers at that level do memorize.
This course is primarily for business people who want to use stories to communicate more effectively
their business goals, their professional goals, their civic goals.
In that case, I do not recommend that you memorize stories.
I'll be honest with you.
I don't memorize my stories.
I tell them a little bit differently each time, but they're still effective because I retain the elements.
I have the same basic elements in the story.
It's easier for me.
It's easier for the audience.
So my recommendation, unless you're a highly paid professional keynote speaker or you're trying to
do something with high levels of theatricality, I do not recommend memorizing because it's just really
hard and it only takes one little glitch and then all of a sudden it's obvious to everyone, Oh, I
forgot what I was trying to memorize.
And it's awkward for everyone.

--- How Do You Remember Your Stories ---

How do you remember what stories to use in a presentation?
Well, my advice is don't try to remember.
That's extra work.
When you're speaking in front of people, you're feeling stress.
And when your body is feeling stressed, your brain is shutting down because your body is pulsating
with adrenaline and it's telling you, get ready to run.
That's the worst time to put extra stress on your memory.
So my recommendation is cheat.
I just use a simple cheat sheet.
Here's a checklist.
This has 23 elements.
These are 23 stories and points.
If I'm going to give an hour long keynote speech, I have several of these around the room.
I've made the font large enough so that I don't have to put any glasses on and off and do all that stuff.
And that way I don't have to remember anything.
I can just glance down at my notes from time to time and I know exactly what story to talk about next.

--- Is It Ever a Bad Idea to Tell a Story ---

Is never a bad idea to tell a story in a presentation.
In my professional opinion.
No, it's not.
As long as you are aware of your time constraints, what the audience's expectations are, and you match
those accordingly.
Again, I've never you heard me say this at the beginning of this course.
I've never heard anyone say about a speaker.
I hated the way that person gave us interesting, relevant stories today about points that are important
to us.
It's possible Someone could say that It's possible.
I've never heard it.
So I don't think you can go wrong by telling a story.
Does that mean every story is going to be great?
No, that's not what I said.

--- Can a Story Backfire ---

Is it possible for stories to hurt you with the audience to backfire?
Absolutely.
Of course it's possible.
Stories are not a panacea.
If you pick a horrible story that your audience doesn't like or they're offended by or it doesn't resonate,
it's not going to help you at all, It can, in fact, damage your reputation.
If you're speaking to an international audience and people outside North America and you want to use
stories that all relate to American football, they're going to be looking at you like you're strange
and weird because you are strange and weird to them.
They have no idea what you're talking about.
If you're telling a story about something that is offensive to someone's religious, ethnic, philosophical
belief system, they're not going to focus on your message or later parts of your story.
They're just going to find you an offensive human being.
So, of course, it's possible for stories to backfire and to hurt you.
But that doesn't mean the problem is with stories.
That means you didn't select the right stories and you didn't test them in advance with the right sorts
of audiences.

--- What Is the Maximum Number of Stories You Can Use ---

What's the most number of stories you could or should tell in a presentation?
I want to step back a moment from that question and ask a different question of you.
Think of the best speaker you've ever seen.
How many messages do you remember?
You heard me talk about this earlier in the course.
I've asked that question for years.
No one's ever had more than five messages they remember from their top speaker.
So if you have extra time, my recommendation is use additional stories to flesh out your main points.
Whether you have one point, two, three, 4 or 5, But don't say, Well, I told three stories.
That's the most you can tell.
Now let me just go on and dump data for the next hour.
It's not how the human brain processes information, so I don't think there is any upper limit of stories.
Although if you're telling 100 stories in ten minutes, chances are you're racing through them.
You're not really putting in all the story elements.
So first and foremost, focus on what it is you want your audience to do.
Then focus on the messages you want them to remember.
Then come up with at least one powerful, interesting, memorable story for each message.
And then if you have time, add additional stories to flesh out your messages.
That's the structure I find helps most people prepare their presentations in the most effective manner.

--- Clintonian Eye Contact ---

When it comes to delivering presentations.
There's basically three types of eye contact.
There's the bottom 1% of speakers.
They are staring at the floor or reading their notes, completely ignoring you or looking at their bullet

They're looking at the room the whole time.

It might be slow, but they're never really looking at you.
They're never really looking at one person at a time.
They're looking at the group.

at them if you're the speaker.

использовать для создания презентаций, но все же, если кто-то хочет увидеть яркие спецэффекты, он может пойти и посмотреть
фильм, снятый в Голливуде, Болливуде или многих других местах.
В наши дни вы им не нужны.
Так что моя рекомендация.
Будьте проще, убедитесь, что у вас есть простые изображения, которые оживляют и запоминают ваше сообщение,
и не тратьте время на анимацию и спецэффекты, и это действительно хорошая причина, чтобы сделать это.
И это помогает людям понять и запомнить сообщение.
Ладно, зачем они рассказывают эту историю, она просто драматизирует то, что иногда мы думаем, что спецэффект
- это действительно круто, но на самом деле это пустая трата времени.
Большую часть времени я пытаюсь убедить людей не использовать спецэффекты в презентациях, потому что, по моему
опыту, в ста процентах случаев вы будете использовать это как предлог, чтобы не репетировать свою презентацию.
Лучше потратить время на репетицию презентации на видео, чтобы убедиться, что она хороша, чем спускаться
в эту черную дыру, потому что, начав с небольшого спецэффекта, даже такого простого,
как порхающая птичка, вы можете подправлять его в течение следующих двух, трех, четырех часов или двух-трех-четырех
дней.
А человеческая природа такова, какова она есть, вы используете это как оправдание, чтобы не практиковаться, не записывать на видео,
не проверять свою речь перед другими людьми.

--- 'I Can't do This' Becomes 'I Can Do This' ---

Or even two people.

--- I Was The Skunk At the Party ---

Context is key quite often when you are making presentations to the news media.
You can say something from your own office or a press conference or speech and maybe nobody cares.
But if you change the context slightly, all of a sudden you get massive attention.
A massive spotlight on your messages.
Case in point, several decades ago, I was a political consultant.
I was doing media training in public speaking training, but also doing general consulting for political
candidates.
I was working with a candidate running for mayor.
He was on the city council in Charlotte, North Carolina, my hometown.
And we found out that the next day he was going to have an opponent announce he was also running for
mayor.
And I thought, well, this seems like a good opportunity.
So we knew in advance for a day that this press conference was going to happen.
So I simply went to the opponent's press conference.
Now, I was polite.
I was well dressed.
I wasn't yelling, I wasn't disruptive.
I didn't have placards, banners that wasn't my style.
But after the candidate announced he was running, I then just walked up to all the TV reporters and
said I was a spokesperson for the other candidate, had a few words to say.
And I said what was good about my candidate and what we thought were the flaws of this announced candidate.
Before you knew it, I was surrounded by TV cameras and reporters.
I got as much media attention as the candidate who announced he was running against my candidate, that
the opposition campaign was furious.
They yelled at me, too bad I didn't lie.
I didn't resort to demagoguery.
I didn't cheat.
In my view.
I certainly didn't do anything unethical.
And it generated a tremendous amount of coverage for my particular candidate.
And my candidate was happy.
I was happy.
So sometimes when you're looking for a way of putting a spotlight on the messages you want to present,
you have to look for the right context.
The media absolutely loves conflict.
So if they see that you are in contrast to another set of ideas, it increases the odds.
You'll get a lot of attention, but you have to be willing to feel a little awkward.
I did feel a little awkward there.
I felt a little rude, but it was highly successful.

--- Why Did You Wear That Ugly Tie ---

Many years ago.
In the late 1980s, I was hosting a weekly TV political talk show.
It was syndicated throughout Florida, and I was living in Tallahassee, Florida, the capital of the
state.
This was back before the days of email and text messaging and all that.
So when you got viewer mail, it was literally mail.
Someone had to write a letter, type it, find an envelope, put a stamp on it.
So, you know, they really wanted to communicate with you.
I'd finished a show one week and I thought, Boy, I did a good job.
I said, So many brilliant, interesting, fascinating things.
I'm sure there's going to be great commentary in the viewer mail.
A couple days go by, go to the mailbox, open it up.
Sure enough, something that's clearly handwritten from a viewer.
I open it up.
Dear T.J., why did you wear that ugly tie last Sunday?
Here.
I thought I had all these brilliant comments people would want to praise me for.
What stuck out was my tie.
Here's what I found in working with people, preparing for TV interviews, being on TV myself.
It's not that there's one perfect thing to wear, but if you have one thing that stands out, that's
the only thing anyone's going to notice or talk about.
So if your tie is loose, if you have jewelry that's so much more interesting than anything you say,
if you've got a collar up, there's anything that stands out.
That's what people will notice.
So it is really important for you to figure out what's the image you're trying to project if you're
not specifically trying to sell yourself as a fashion designer or an artist or a really creative type,
and you're not in a specific job like doctor wearing a doctor's outfit or firemen and a fireman's outfit.
If you're just a typical business person or someone in government, then in general, you need to dress
in a way that's somewhat bland and doesn't distract people.
It's not that you can't have personality, but you don't want to distract them.
And that was the problem.
I wore a tie.
I think it had Paisley, so it had too many colors, too many small patterns.
It jumped around and it just captured too much attention.
Okay, so why do I tell that story?
I tell that story during a day of media training when I'm instructing people on what to wear for TV
because I want to drive home the importance of really thinking about what you're wearing because you

You do what?
Everything goes according to plan.

--- Less Is More ---

I was working with a very well known politician.
He had been the speaker of the legislature of a major Southern state.
He was now running for another office and was about to announce in the next couple of days.
I was brought in as his media consultant and media trainer.
We're sitting there in his home going over a standard media training.
What I always do, getting comfortable on how you look on TV, then talking about the messaging.
So if you're running for office, part of your message has to answer the question Why are you running
for this office?
So I asked him that question and he said, Well, because I want to do this and I want to do this and
I want to do this, I want to do this, and I'm trying to keep up writing it down.
We're putting it on poster boards.
We're writing it down.
Before you knew it, the house was practically covered with messages as to why he wanted to run.
Now, he fancied himself a very serious public policy person, very intellectual.
But when I asked him, Why are you running for office, he had to say hundreds and hundreds of things.
Now, once you're in office, there are hundreds of things you have to do, maybe thousands, but you
can't run on a platform of doing hundreds of things for candidates and for all the other voters in your
district.
It just doesn't work that way.
So and this was my fault as a trainer.
It was fairly early in my training business, my my training career before, you know what?
We had spent five, six hours brainstorming on messages.
So now we have to do the compression down to three messages quickly, and he wouldn't do it and he wouldn't
do it and he wouldn't do it.
We almost had to just arbitrarily pick three.
And then we had about five minutes to practice interviews and practices.
Three messages did not end well.
What happened during the campaign when he was interviewed, his announcement and every other time,
every time he spoke, he said something different.
Every time someone asked him, why are you running for office, he said ten new things.
Nothing ever resonated.
And he lost his bid for public office.
Now, I'm not proud of how that training went.
I'd like to think I've learned a lot since then.
I now impose a very strict discipline on how much time you could spend on brainstorming messages.
But a lot of times people have this mistaken notion that, Oh, I don't want to dumb things down.
I'm a smart person.
I want to respect the audience.
All that's great, but it actually takes more intellect to put your messages in priority than it does
to just dump them all out on a table.
When you have 500 messages, there's really no difference between that and having no message.
So why do I tell that story?
I want people to realize you don't get extra credit as a candidate or anyone trying to communicate to
the public by more and more, more and more and more.
You cannot spend a disproportionate amount of your time in the brainstorming mode.
That's the easiest thing to do for most people.
It's fun.
It's intellectually interesting, but it doesn't help you actually communicate.
You've got to spend as much time, if not more time, narrowing your messages to the top three, coming
up with soundbites leaving time for rehearsal.
If not, you're going to end up losing, whether at the ballot box or at the cash register.

--- Familiarity Breeds Contempt ---

--- Sometimes, Experience Just Means You Are Old ---

One day I was conducting a media training session in my New York City studio, and it was with the premier
of Bermuda, the top politically elected leader of the country.
We were doing a simple press conference and I do what I always do.
I ask tough questions.
We record it, we play it back, we critique it.
And I said, Mr. Prime Minister, what about and I asked some sort of generic tough question.
I'll never forget his answer.
He said, I reject the premise of your question.
It's a ridiculous question.
Next question with an angry look on his face.
And then we went to the next question.
We finished that that little segment, and I pulled aside his aide once and I said, Is that really
how he answers the questions?
They said, yes.
I said, Does he ever do interviews?
They said, yeah, he does dozens of interviews every single week.
What was his profession before he entered politics?
He ran a public relations firm.
I was just shocked.
Now, I quickly showed him that that isn't in his advantage to answer questions that way.
It's confrontational, makes it look like he's hiding something, creates a clash with reporters.
And what I coached him to do, what I coach all of my clients to do, is not to dodge questions, but
to simply focus on the part of the premise of the question you can deal with and answer it in your own
positive terms.
Or if someone says something you think is flatly wrong, you can say actually and then state what you
do believe and let the person deduce you don't agree with their premise.
This way there's no confrontation.
You're not saying anything quotable off message, and it doesn't seem like you're on the defensive any
time you're defending with the media, you're basically losing.
Show them that technique.
Complete difference, complete sea change of how he came across.
It turned press conferences from an adversarial contentious to smooth pleasant affairs.
So remember, if you hear a question you don't like.
That's okay.
But rewrite it in your own brain.
Don't tell the reporter you think the premise is ridiculous.
Just alter the premise to one you think is fair and honest and answer that.
Okay.
What did I do with that story?
What I was trying to do is convey that even someone who's really experienced in the media, even someone

--- Ronald Reagan ---

Ronald Reagan, the great communicator.

He was an actor.
He's a natural at it.
No, when Ronald Reagan had to give a really important speech like a State of the Union address, he
had a tremendous discipline.
First of all, he would meet with his staff members, his speechwriters for months, going through ideas
for the speech.
He would then come up with ideas, look at drafts, give notes, give feedback.
He then would force them to finish the speech one week before it was due.
This way he's not doing last minute edits five minutes before the speech is given.
It gave him time to read it out loud every night for hours for a week before the State of the Union
address.
Not to memorize it, just to get more familiar with the words, to build a bond with the words, to
build a relationship with the words, to get really comfortable with the whole speech.
But even that wasn't enough.
He would then spend an entire day doing videotaped rehearsal with the speech so that when he was reading
the words off the teleprompter, it didn't seem like he was reading words off the teleprompter.
It felt like he was just speaking to you from the heart.
Now, Ronald Reagan obviously knew about stagecraft since he was an actor.
He gave tremendous importance to every aspect of how things looked.
For example, you would never see Ronald Reagan walking up to a lectern holding his speech the way you
would see George Bush or others.
He wanted to create the illusion of just talking to people.
So what he did is he had his notes mostly on note cards three by five, four by six note cards.
He would have them in his left suit pocket.
So when he walked up on stage and got behind a lectern, he could walk with his hands free.
He could get up there, wave with with one hand, pull the notes out without anyone seeing it, put
it on the lectern, then wave with the other hand and that his notes are in front of him.
Nobody ever saw him touch his notes.
He was then careful to start off by looking at people, then dipping down to look at his notes.
He is one of the few politicians who was actually good at reading from notes and delivering a speech.
Most people can't do that masterful, masterful communicator for big speeches.
He did practice a lot, but he was also good on the fly.
If there was an emergency like the Challenger shuttle exploding and he had to address the nation, he
could do it really well quickly then, too.
But he's someone who didn't take it for granted when he knew it was a big speech.
He knew he had time.
He would work on it, craft it.
Now, as president, he obviously had speechwriters, but Reagan was a good writer himself before he
became president.
He did daily five minute political commentaries on radio, sometimes television.
He wrote them out by hand himself, and he spoke constantly.

It's about what's interesting to the audience.

--- Eliminating Speaking Anxiety ---

If you have a fear of public speaking, relax.
It just means you're normal.
Most people have a fear of public speaking.
In fact, numerous polls have shown that the number one fear people have is public speaking.
So it's actually kind of weird if you don't fear public speaking, as Jerry Seinfeld always points out.
Because of this poll, it means most people, if they had to go to a funeral, would rather be in the
casket than delivering the eulogy.
Now, I think that is going too far.
I think most people, if you said, all right, you have to jump out of this plane without a parachute
or jump off this cliff or give a short speech, most people would be very happy to give that speech.
But I do think that giving a speech is one of those things that the average person could be asked to
do in the course of a normal week is the thing that creates a lot of tension that makes them uncomfortable.
So I do understand why people say they fear public speaking.
But I've got a little test for you right now.
If I said to you, you're going to go to a restaurant tonight and see your three best friends, it's
going to be a noisy, crowded restaurant.
There'll be a lot of people around and you're going to talk to your best friends about the game you
all saw last night that you care about or a particular movie you all saw in the last week.
And everyone's passionate about it.
And now it's your turn to talk about what you thought of it.
And you've got a glass of wine or whatever you enjoy.
Now, are you nervous when you're talking?
Chances are no.
Well, guess what?
That's public speaking.
You're in a room.
There are a lot of people there and your mouth is moving.
You're speaking and you say, Well, TJ, that's different.
I'm relaxed.
I'm with friends.
It really isn't different.
The reason you're comfortable is, you know, how you're coming across.
You're feeling relaxed.
But the fact that there's a room full of people and your mouth is moving and sound is coming in, that's
not actually making you nervous, but you are doing public speaking.
Now, why do I point that out?
It's because I believe most people who are nervous about public speaking are nervous in a narrower context.
They're nervous about speaking in public, in school or in business, or they're not quite sure how
they're coming across and they're not quite sure if the information they're presenting is interesting
to anyone or is understandable to anyone.
If you're talking about the big game last night that you saw and you saw it with your buddies or your
friends, you know they understand what you're talking about.
There's that sense of commonality.
And yet if you're giving a new business pitch or if you're talking to an angel investor or a venture
capitalist about why this person should fund your organization for $1 million, you may be feeling really
scared and nervous.
But I want to suggest to you it's not really about public speaking.
It's really more about this particular situation of do I have an interesting message?
Are they going to like me?
Those are separate issues.
If you absolutely, positively can never speak in public.
If you go to a restaurant with your family members and you can't talk at all because you're just so
afraid of people around, I'm afraid this course isn't for you.
I'm not going to be able to help you.
But if you're like most people where you are comfortable in certain situations but then deathly afraid
in other situations, this course is really going to help you.
Now, let's take a step back.
Why are we nervous when we speak?
Evolutionary biologists believe that human beings are programmed to fear being separated from the crowd.
It's a defense mechanism.
In prehistoric days, if you're a part of the herd, it doesn't matter if you're gazelle or deer or
human beings.
If you're away from the herd, you're vulnerable.
Some lion or tiger bear can see just you zoom in on you, grab you, kill you and eat you.
So when you're standing up to speak the whole herd, you were with the audience.
They're over there.
You're now standing.
You're the only person everyone can see.
So from an evolutionary biological standpoint, it makes sense to be nervous.
So your body is sending adrenaline throughout everywhere in your veins.
And because of that, your brain is shutting down because your body is saying don't think run.
And that's why if you've ever noticed, your palms might get wet, If you weren't wearing shoes, you
would notice the bottoms of your feet are getting wet.
That's because your body is preparing you for flight.
Your body is preparing you to run away from what it senses is a dangerous situation.
You being isolated from the crowd now.
The good news is, even though on some college campuses, the audience can be rude or heckle.
It's highly unlikely that any audience member is going to come attack you, physically attack you and
kill you and eat you.
It's just not likely to happen.
So at some level, we've got to hide that from our own sense and not worry about it and instead focus
what we've really got to do, and that is speak in a way that's interesting and understandable and relevant
to your audience.
The number one way to get over being afraid of speaking is you've got to focus exclusively on your audience,
helping them.
If you're really focused on helping your audience understand something, learn something you haven't
even had the luxury of thinking about yourself at that point, your nerves will melt away.

--- Save Time by Focusing On Your Exact Goal ---

If I say to you, get in the car, drive, let's just go for a trip.
You might ask, Well, where are we going?
Are we going to drive across the country to California?
Are we going to drive around the block?
Fair questions.
Because if you don't know where you're going, if you don't have a destination in mind, you're going
to go around in circles, get lost, just meander.
You're not going to accomplish much.
Well, the same thing happens with speeches, with presentations.
Far too often, people just start off with a speech with a vague fuzzy notion of a topic, and they
think, Well, how can I gather everything I know about the topic?
And that is the root cause of all of your problems all of the time suck when it comes to your speech.
Because if you just go off with a general vague notion of telling people everything about that subject
or everything your company has done in the last six months or everything your government organization
does, you're just going to dig more and more and more data and it's just you're going to be lost.
So, so much of what I'm going to stress here in this course is all hinging around this one thing right
now.
You've got to make a decision right at the beginning of this speech preparation.
Are you going to do it the way you've always done it before, which is just well, let's start with
the research and gather stuff.
Or are you going to start with the goal in mind if you know that today you're in New York City and you
want to drive to Los Angeles and get there the quickest way possible, driving the fewest miles possible
on the best roads, you would spend some time planning, you would perhaps get a good GPS and you would
go there.
You wouldn't just say, Well, let me just drive around the block and let me see where the sun is.
And oh, this looks like a nice road.
You'd never get there, or you would take you months to get there instead of a few days.
It's exactly the same thing with the speech.
So here's what I want you to do for every speech you ever give in the future before you start doing
anything, before you even pull up a PowerPoint slide software I want you to write down.
It can be on a single sheet of paper.
It could be on your computer screen first thing.
What is it you want this audience to do after hearing your speech?
One sentence What do you want them to do?
If you're in business, then you probably want them to become a client, to request a meeting with you
to authorize a budget to approve findings you've already done in research.
What is it you want them to do?
If it's a government agency and you're trying to encourage people to eat more vegetables, what's the
specific action?
Now, keep in mind, most of the time when people give presentations, the audience doesn't do anything
except a fall asleep or B, check their email.
So if you actually get some members of the audience to do anything, you're going to be wildly successful
compared to most speakers.
If you get most of the people in the audience to do something, you are going to be one of the most
successful speakers that audience has seen in a long time.
So that's the starting point.
Do that before you do anything else.
Do that before you even get to a computer.
Just write down one sentence.
What is it you want this audience to do after hearing your presentation?

--- Learn the Secret to Communicating Effectively Using a Teleprompter ---

--- Potential Disasters ---

There are a lot of different kinds of teleprompters these days.
Some of them you can adjust with an old fashioned knob yourself, some of them with a mouse, some of
them with a foot pedal, and others you have an actual teleprompter operator, someone else doing it
for you.
There are pitfalls with all of these, and there are certain things you need to do to protect yourself.
And I want to go over some of those steps right now so that you're not left unguarded.
If you are going to have another teleprompter operator moving it, you've got to rehearse with that
person and you have to make sure that person is following you.
Otherwise you get back to the same speed, the same tone.
The reason people do this is they are afraid that the words are going to go off the screen and they
won't know what to say.
So you have to be in sync with your teleprompter operator.
If you pause, they better stop because if they keep rolling and you're pausing, you're up a creek
without a paddle, you are in big, big trouble.
So you need to find somebody who's reliable, someone willing to practice with you, or you got to think
twice about even using a teleprompter.
The next thing you have to be prepared for is a teleprompter is used as a part of a computer, even
if it's an iPhone.
Guess what about computers?
They break, they have glitches, they malfunction.
They like electricity.
They get bugs in them.
All of which to say is you still need to have your speech on paper or at least notes.
I prefer having notes consolidated on a single sheet, but if you really want to get every single word
just right, you better have it all on paper because paper doesn't require electricity.
Paper doesn't have glitches on it typically, so it's a good fallback.
I hope you don't have to use it, but it's there if you need it.
There's all sorts of problems that can happen with computers.
Most famously, when Bill Clinton was president and giving his 1995 State of the Union.
What happened was it was uploaded into the teleprompter software as State of the Union.
When the person uploaded it, it said, Do you want to delete State of the Union?
No.
Why do I want to do that?
I'm putting it in so person put no.
And there it was.

The whole world is watching whispers to Vice President Gore and says, Call Stephanopoulos and get the
correct speech.
We have last year's speech.
Now, Bill Clinton even then was an extraordinarily.

--- Reasons Not to Use a Teleprompter ---

There's a topic I wanted to address at the very beginning of this course, but I didn't want to turn
you off.
I didn't want to scare you away.
But the topic is what is your decision process for actually deciding to use a teleprompter?
Again, there are plenty of good reasons to use a teleprompter if you're a newscaster every day, Well,
you've got to use one.
There's no way you can get the names and the facts straight of brand new stories of news that just happened.
Yes.
If you're giving a political speech and millions and millions of people are watching you and you've
got exactly seven minutes and 28 seconds for your slot on prime time, that may be a good reason.
But many people use a teleprompter because they think it gives them greater control.
Not really, because if you do a bad job on the teleprompter, you're not controlling the outcome.
The outcome of any speech is not what comes out of your mouth.
It's what do people remember, What do they retain?
So they can act upon it.
So if you're reading a teleprompter and a wooden, stiff, phony way, the only outcome is people have
a negative impression of you and don't remember anything you said.
So that's an illusion to think that that's somehow safer.
It's not safer and it's not saving you time.
Many people use a teleprompter because they think it will save the prep time.
As we talked about in the previous lecture, it doesn't save time for most people.
Most of the time they're far better off using a simple page of notes to speak for most business executives
in the world and for that matter, most politicians.
The real danger of a speech is not that they got one word wrong, one comma wrong, and suddenly there's
tremendous criticism that does happen for presidents of countries or heads of of federal banking systems
that can happen.
But for most people, most of the time, the biggest problem in our speech is not that we got one word
wrong and there's a lot of criticism.
The biggest danger for most of us is we're so boring, nobody remembers anything we said.
So that's why I would urge you focus your time on making your speeches interesting and memorable.
And I've got other courses to deal with that.
That's not the point of this course, but that should be your focus.
Having an interesting speech and delivering it in the best possible way, don't use a teleprompter because
everyone else is.
Don't use a teleprompter because there is some technician who's sort of running the conference and says,
Well, everyone else is.
You have to.
It'll be there.
The only reason to use a teleprompter is you've decided that will help you communicate most effectively
with your audience.
That's the only reason to use a teleprompter.
So, for example, I've been speaking to you for this entire course and I'm not using a teleprompter.
