So I know this.
So I didn't use a teleprompter.
So please give real thought to what is the best way for you to communicate with your audience.
And it may in fact be notes and not using a teleprompter, but make the judgment based on what will
help the audience, not what might save you time.

--- Secrets from Reagan ---

You heard me mention at the beginning the reason to use a teleprompter is not to save time, but to
really make sure everything goes right and you get the exact wording and phrasing the way you want it.
Now, people think of Ronald Reagan as one of the great communicators of all time.
He was called the Great Communicator.
Regardless of your politics.
Most fair minded people would say Ronald Reagan was a great speaker.
Now, many assume that was because he was an actor and had a lot of experience in front of cameras.
That's partially it.
But the real reason is he brought an actor's discipline of rehearsal to the public speaking process.
So when Reagan had a major speech like the State of the Union address, he would practice the speech
out loud for three hours a night for a week.
Now, he wasn't doing that to memorize the speech.
He was using a teleprompter.
He was doing that to build a comfort with the words, a relationship with the words to get his brain
and mouth and everything in sync.
Used to having those words come out of his mouth in a set way.
After all that practice out loud, he would still spend an entire day practicing on video with the teleprompter.
Again, not doing it to memorize, but doing it so he could get the pauses just right, the emphasis
just right, the head movements just right.
So if Ronald Reagan could spend a whole day doing videotape rehearsal for his teleprompter speeches,
what's your excuse for not spending at least an hour doing it?
There's always time for anything that's important.
If there's no time to practice your speech, your teleprompter speech on video, maybe you shouldn't
make time to give the speech at all.
So please, please practice on video.
That's the real secret of the master communicators.

--- Tricks for Look Good on Camera - Presentation Skills ---

The next thing you have to remember is you've got to lean forward a little bit.
Now I'm standing for this.

--- Learn the Secret to Speaking to Large Audiences ---

I've got good news and I've got bad news.
The good news is it's actually pretty easy to speak in front of large crowds.
A thousand.
5000.
100,000.

What happens is we tense up.
Our heart starts racing.
We get scared, our brain stops working, our memory stops working, and our body's telling us, run
our hands get sweaty.
Well, why is that?
It is important.

evolutionary biologists believe we as human beings are hardwired to fear public speaking because public
speaking is essentially being separated from the crowd, separated from the herd.
In prehistoric times, if we are in the jungle and we're a part of the herd, there's safety in numbers.
If there's 2000 other water buffalo with us or any sort of animal and a lion or a tiger bear comes,
our odds are pretty good one will get it of the herd.
But the other 1999 we'll be safe.
So there's safety in numbers.
The old cliche is true.
If we're completely separated from the herd or if we're just all alone in the open field and animals
and other other predators of ours can see us from every direction.
We're vulnerable.
We could be eaten, attacked.
That's not good.
So that's why many scientists believe that we as human beings are so nervous about speaking, especially
in front of large crowds.
That's why our bodies react differently.
That's why our hands get wet.
Moisture is coming out.
Moisture is coming out of our feet, too, because our body is telling us, don't think run.
Now, you may have noticed if you're ever trying to turn the page of a book, if you go like that,
there's more friction.
It's easier to turn that page the same way if you all of a sudden have to run through a jungle for your
life.
Having moisture coming out of your hands at the palm of your feet gives you more traction.
You can grab vines, swing away, and it's better for protection.
Your body is telling you run.
You've got that adrenaline rush, more energy.
But that's also when your body isn't working well from the neck up.

is telling you to spend all of your energy running.
And it makes perfect sense.
S If you're in the jungle about to be attacked, unfortunately, if you're about to give a speech in

When it comes to speaking in front of large audiences.

--- Pause for Maximum Affect and Impact ---

Here's one thing that is a little different about speaking in front of large audiences.
The difference is you need a little more of a pause between your big thoughts.
It takes a while for your sound to simply travel all the way around a large room, regardless of the
number of speakers.
And there occasionally could be an echo.
You help yourself by having a little more of a pause between your thoughts, a little more of a transition.
It allows the sound to filter out through the room.
It allows people to process it.
Part of it is they can't see your lips and your mouth as well as if it were just a room of 20 people
speaking.
There are fewer visual cues, although there may be a big image magnification.
Still, you'll make it easier for people easier to digest if you pause a little longer between thoughts
between paragraphs and if you just speak a little bit slower than usual, it's just easier for your
words to flow through the room or through the audience.
So keep that in mind with the speed, especially given that you might be nervous.
And when we're nervous, we tend to speak faster than usual.
So slow it down.
More pauses.

--- What Makes a TED Talk ---

So you want to be a TEDx speaker?
For starters, let's figure out what actually is a TEDx speaker.
It's really just someone who gives a speech or a presentation.
That's interesting when you think about it, because after all, most speakers in the world at most
conventions, at most conferences, the lecture halls of most universities are boring.
They're way too long.
They're way too boring, and nobody remembers anything.
Now, this course is going to go into a lot of very specific details of things that most TEDx presentations
have.
But before you get into the specifics of how this exact 17 minutes or this walking around on the stage,
you've got to really step back and ask yourself, do you have something interesting to say?
It can't just be a really good sales pitch on why to buy my paper for your copy machine.
Now, if you've got some way of creating paper out of trees and it doesn't chop down trees and it solves
the energy crisis and it's completely biodegradable in a way that doesn't cause any landfill problem,
well then maybe you have the elements of a TEDx speech, but simply buy my product because it delivers
a greater value.
That's not a TEDx speech.
Ideas worth spreading.
That's the slogan of they do take it very, very seriously.
One of the reasons TEDx is successful as an organization is they have the discipline to say no because
most trade associations, most conferences all over the world, they let people speak because they have
political influence or because of their stature in the industry or because they underwrite it or they're
sponsors or because they have high name ID or because they're famous.
All sorts of reasons people get invited to give speeches at organizations.
TEDx is different if you can't actually deliver an interesting speech and deliver it well, they don't
care who you are.
You're not going to speak because of that.
They have a better brand, a better reputation than, frankly, anyone I can think of when it comes
to a forum just for speakers.
If you're like me, you probably watch a lot of TEDx speeches because it's frankly more interesting
than what you see on regular television.
And you can watch it on your smart TV, on your cell phone, on your tablet and anywhere.
And even if it's not a topic that you're fascinated by, you always learn one thing.
There's always something compelling.
There's something that kind of changes your thought process and it never goes on and on and on too long.
You know, it's going to be for a set amount of time and it's typically going to be less than 20 minutes.
That's the beauty of TEDx.
So if you want to be a TEDx speaker, you've got to first step back and ask yourself, Do you really
have something that's genuinely interesting?
Do you have something that is an idea worth spreading?
If you don't have that, you can still be a great public speaker.
You can be a great sales presenter, you can be a good spokesperson, you can be a good CEO.
You might not be a good candidate to speak at TEDx.
So that's the first thing you've got to do, is really step back and ask yourself, Do you fundamentally
have an idea worth spreading?

--- Passion for an Idea Worth Spreading ---

Do you have a great idea that the world absolutely must know about and have a huge passion for sharing
it?
If you don't have both of those things, you're probably not going to be invited to speak at Ted.
Now, I know this is a course on how to speak at Ted, but I would caution you, I really don't think
it's particularly productive to just sit down and say, you know, I want to write a speech for Ted
today because I think it would be prestigious.
It would make me look cool.
It would make my friends think I'm smart if I spoke at Ted.

Anyone who will listen to them.

And he may get $200,000 a speech when he gives that talk now.

--- Tell a Story ---

TEDx presentations are very different from most presentations at corporations conferences meetings,
because most corporations have speakers who give big, long, boring data dumps.
Facts.
Fact.
Bullet point, Bullet point.
And the speaker tries to do too much.
They overwhelm their audience with so much data, it's boring.
Everyone is pulling out their cell phones and checking their email and nobody really pays attention.
A TEDx speech is different.
In part, they simply impose a discipline on speakers of don't try to communicate more than a handful
of ideas.
And I mean really no more than a handful.
Sometimes just one idea because then you have the time to tell a story.
All great TEDx speakers have stories.
I don't mean that they're funny stories.
I don't mean that they're necessarily wildly dramatic and involve shootings or death, but they're recounting
real experiences.
A recent TEDx speaker, I saw a woman talking about her experiences in the music industry and how the
music industry can evolve.
Talks very specifically about her personal interactions with real fans.
One came up to her and said, Here's a $10 bill.
I want you to have this.
I feel embarrassed.
I stole your music from a friend's CD and I didn't pay you, and I want you to have it.
She gave personal stories, fleshing out her point.
Her point is people in the music industry have to make their customers care and want to compensate artists.

It has to be about getting actual music lovers to care enough to give to the artist.
And she had compelling story after story after story to make it come alive.
If you want to be a TEDx speaker or someone who's good enough to be a TEDx speaker, the biggest difference
between awful speakers and TEDx speakers is TEDx speakers have great stories.
Not just at the beginning of the speech, not just at the end of the speech, not just to manipulate
people, but for every important idea they have a story to flesh it out because people can visualize
it and their mind's eye, they can relate to it, they can understand it, and they can remember it.
So when you come up with your idea and your main mission of what you want to accomplish in your presentation,
you have got to have stories that involve real conversations with real people about real problems.
And one of them needs to be you, how you felt, how it was resolved, what the outcome was.
And you can say, well, there was no time.
I only have 12 minutes or I only have 17 minutes.
You do have time because the story is not an extra.
It's not a frivolous little dessert.

remember it.

If you have to cut something, you cut the additional points.

But what is absolutely essential, what is not a luxury, are stories that really dramatize the problems
you're solving and showing You're living it and experiencing it that way.
Your audience doesn't have just an intellectual understanding of the problems you're dealing with.
They can see it, feel it, taste it, touch it, and have an emotional connection with it.
That's what you need to be a TEDx speaker or a good speaker anywhere, any time.

--- Plan Your Visuals ---

If you're going to have a great TEDx speech, you need to think of the visuals now.
TEDx is very different from most conferences, and they simply have no tolerance for awful boring visuals.
You cannot go to them and say, Here's my PowerPoint deck of 30 slides and 12 bullet points on each
slide.
What the people at TEDx know is that audiences around the world do not really enjoy watching someone
speak and then having to read a bunch of text up on the slide, whether they are in person in the room
where the speech is given or watching later online on YouTube or at the TEDx site.
What they understand is people like visuals.
So if you're going to use visuals, it needs to be a picture, an image.
It could be something you actually hold up.
It could be a prop.
If you're going to use visuals, don't be lazy.
The laziest thing in the world to do is to just type a bunch of bullet points, text it, won't cut
it for TEDx and frankly, it won't cut it anywhere.
If you really want audiences to understand you and remember you, text is boring.
If you want people to read, give them a book, email them later.
Don't just give them a bunch of stuff up on a slide so you don't have to have visuals for your TEDx
presentation.
Do keep that in mind.
Your ideas need to stand on their own.
Your stories need to paint pictures in your audience's mind, and it could be just the background that
they have for the particular forum that day and the staging that works for you.
You don't have to have visuals, but the question to ask is not whether you need visuals.
No one cares about you.
The Speaker The question is, do you have some visuals that will help your audience understand the concept
better?
Remember the concept better when Al Gore is talking about global warming, he's showing a picture.
Here's what the glacier looked like 30 years ago.
Here's what it looks like today.
One's covered with a lot of snow and ice.
One has a lot of green on it.
The visuals make his point in a much more powerful way than simply putting statistics of ice cap melting
2% a year.
You've got to have visuals that make your case in a way that people can look at it, see it, understand
it.
So the rule of thumb for any visual, does it make your audience understand your point better than you

Does it make them remember it better than you saying it?
If you can't say yes to both, they're lousy visuals, get rid of them.
But put some real thought into this.
The folks at Ted do a fantastic job of staging of lighting the opening sound effects.
They're making this thing look like a slick production.
And this could be the one time you speak in your entire life where more than a million people see it.

But come up with that right picture a graph that's really, really simple and focuses on just one idea

Think about your visuals and make sure it helps your audience do that.

--- Your Message Can Move Millions ---

If you want to be a motivational speaker.

people understand you but feel you.
They have to connect with you, the head and the heart level.

--- Finding What Is So Special About You ---

--- Give Your Memory a Break With This Tip - Focus on 5 Points ---

--- Writing a Speech Public Speaking ---

What is the best way to write a speech?

You professional speechwriters are not going to like this.

If you actually have to give a speech and my advice is do not write a speech out word for word, it's

It's time consuming.
If you write it all out and you get a little bit nervous, there's this tendency to start reading.
And what reads well doesn't necessarily sound good to the ear.
My recommendation is come up with bullet points.
Come up with a list of your top five ideas, your main ideas, and have a sentence fragment three,
4 or 5 words to remind you of what the concept is.
If there are a couple of facts statistics you need listed under that, and then a few words to tell
you a story associated with that and to work from notes and outline.
It's much, much more effective for most people.
Most of the time I'm not trying to give something that's a solution for everyone 100% of the time,
but if you have to give any sort of business presentation, political speech, anything that is not

you, then I would recommend don't write out the whole speech, come up with ideas, work from a single
sheet of notes, and then practice on video.
Far more important than writing the speech out perfectly word for word.

--- How can I find out whether my presentation worked? ---

So how can you find out if your speech or presentation was effective?
This is actually quite easy, and I'll tell you why.
By the way, it always bugs me when people talk about public speaking skills as a soft skill, like
soft, like a puppy.
It somehow, you know, like judging finger painting.
No, it's not.
Public speaking is just as easy to quantify as any aspect of accounting or physics.
Let me tell you how.
All you have to do, if you want to know if your speech is effective, is ask your audience afterwards.
But you have to ask them the right question.
Ask them what messages they remember from your presentation.
If they remember all of your key messages, you were effective.
If they don't remember, you were ineffective.
Same way you test if your slides are effective.
When you're done, ask your audience what PowerPoint slides.
They remember any slide they remember.
As long as they connect it to the point it was effective.
If they cannot remember your slide, it was ineffective.
Throw it in the trash can or give it as a handout, but don't use it in your actual presentation.
So if you've got a big presentation to 30 important clients on Thursday, get three colleagues, perhaps
people who work in different departments together at lunch on Tuesday, give them your presentation
in the lunch room.
When you're done, don't ask them What do they think?
Because they're going to want to be nice.
They're going to say, Oh, good job, Jim.
Great job, Sally.
Go get them.
That's not helpful advice.
Ask them what messages do they remember?
And because they can't lie about that, they can lie about whether they think you did a good job or
not, or whether you looked professional.
But ask them what messages they remember.
If they don't remember your messages, then you know you're not effective.
You've got to go back to the drawing board.
It's very easy to find out.
Now, also when you're giving a speech for real and people come up to you afterwards, if you're talking
to more than 20 people, typically someone will come up and say, Oh, good job today, good presentation.
What most of us do is we say, Oh, thanks, thanks a lot.
Now you can still do that.
But what I would recommend is then say, hey, thanks, tell me what stands out, What do you remember?
So when I do that and someone says, Well, you know, TJ, you were just so professional and you were
commanding and authoritative and you didn't have any ums.
And your real inspiration is somebody says that to me after a presentation.
I then know I was a complete, utter failure.
Because those weren't my messages.
If they can't tell me specific messages, examples, stories, case studies, I failed miserably.
So don't be afraid to ask people who come up to you after a presentation with any kind of feedback.
What do you remember?
That's honest feedback that you can take to the bank.

Do you care if the person is happy to be there?

So most people.

They figure, Oh, the speaker hasn't really started.
I'm not really missing anything.
And you know what?

Here's the problem, though.

Thank you very much.
What an honor to be here.
Blah, blah, blah.

--- Communicate Effectively By Focusing on Your Top Three Messages ---

So what are your communication goals for this panel appearance?
And it shouldn't be so low as to just be, Well, I want people to think I'm smart and I know about

That is a low bar.

That's the easiest way to get people to remember and perceive you as smart.

If you're a part of a panel and there's debate and there's lots of going back and forth.
Five is too many.
I would focus on no more than three ideas.
And you can put these ideas forth in your prepared talks.
You can also bridge back to them during the question and answer part.

But what's really important here today is boom, boom, boom.

So when you do have that opening five minutes to give your overall position on the issues of the day,

Focus on the ideas you care about most.
So that's what I want you to do.
Now write down three sentences, ten words or less.

--- How to Manage Time When Giving a Presentation ---

So how do you manage time when giving a speech or presentation?
For starters, you should have a pretty good sense of how long it takes you to give the presentation
because you should have rehearsed on video.
And these days that can be as simple as talking to your own cell phone, recording it and looking at
the time.
So this idea that it's impossible to have any idea of how long your speech takes just isn't true.
Now, the worst thing you can do is time your speech by reading it silently to yourself.
Because a speech that takes a half hour to give to people in the real world, you can read silently
to yourself in eight minutes.
So that's not going to have any relationship to the actual length of your presentation.
Now, when you're speaking, you need to factor in more time when there's an audience there because
they may have questions, there may be reactions.
You may see someone looking at you.
They don't quite get it.
You have to go in and explain deeper.
You also want to allocate time in most situations for questions and answers.
So if you're told you've got an hour, I wouldn't prepare 60 minutes worth of content, I would prepare
40 minutes of content and leave time for questions and leave some time for spontaneity and the ability
to go into more detail based on what the audience says.
Now, there are several ways of managing your time when you're in the middle of a presentation.
For starters, most cell phones have a timer function.
You can get a timer app, so you can have that in fairly large font sitting on a table, a lectern near
you.
You could do what I do.
I simply remove my watch and I put it on a table so I can glance down if they're not clocks around.
Here's the thing.
If you speak often enough and I recommend that you try to speak every opportunity you can, you won't
be as nervous when you're not nervous, you won't lose track of time.
If you're completely nervous and feeling tense, that's when you lose all perspective of time.
You can think you're talking for ten minutes and it's really been 50.
Or you can think you've been talking for 50 minutes and you look down and you've been speaking for seven
minutes and you've got to somehow fill up the next 53 minutes and that's when panic occurs.
You don't want that to happen.
So practice, rehearse on video and also have eyesight to clocks, watches or timers.
Do that and you'll be in good shape.
Also remember, though, if you speak and you finish a little bit early, but you've really delivered
the goods, you've given people great content and answer their questions, nobody's going to get upset
if you only took 25 minutes and they told you you had 30 minutes.

--- Become the Master of the Short Story ---

Typically when you are part of a panel discussion, you're not using PowerPoint slides.

You're not going to be able to put up PowerPoint slides.
Most likely, unlikely.
You can give handouts in the middle of a panel discussion.

--- How to Make Your Presentation Memorable Public Speaking ---

So how do you make a presentation memorable?
There are two main ways.
The first is you've got to have compelling, interesting stories, not made up stories, not stories
from a book, but stories about your actual conversations with real people, colleagues, clients,
customers, family members, stories that relate to the message that's important to your audience.
The next thing is you have to bring some passion to this subject.
Those are the two things that people remember over and over again.
As I ask clients from six continents, from all over the world, what speeches do you remember?
What do you remember about them?
That's what I hear again and again.
Interesting stories.
The passion someone had for their subject matter.
That's what will make your speech memorable.
What's going to not make your speech memorable is having all the bullet points.
Just so having the logo perfectly centered on your PowerPoint, that's not going to do it.
You've got to have these compelling stories and deliver it in a way where you're reliving the emotion.
So, for example, I don't tell somebody, Oh, I've been on thousands of talk shows and some have been
difficult.
That's abstract.
Or I don't just say that.
I then tell a story about the time I was down in Florida on a talk radio show, political show, and
the host pulls a gun on me on the air, and I was scared out of my mind.
Now, to find out more details, you'll have to listen to more of these videos.
But that's a story people remember once I flesh out more details.

--- Other Tips to Make You Great - Sitting Standing Notes ---

I recommend hold yourself up high, lean forward and be gesturing, moving your hands when you speak.
That's what I recommend doing.
Don't slump over Now.
Another scenario is directors chairs.
I've seen this at many, many conferences.
Everyone's on a director's chair and depending on how long you have, if it's an opening five minutes

You can get better eye contact.
You get more people focusing on you, eye contact back at you.

It shows you're serious about it and it works very well.

Another scenario is there's a lectern.

But I've also been in many conferences where there's only 25, 30 people in the room, so there's no

The microphone might not even be on if there's only 25 people in the room.
When it's your turn to speak, just walk up, get as close as possible to the first row, speak to people,

Now, a word about notes.

You've robbed the audience of eye contact.
You don't seem very passionate about it and you don't seem like much of an expert.
The other thing that looks odd is having notes on a napkin.

I would recommend either no notes or my first choice have notes on a single sheet of paper, large font,

Extra large font, a single sheet of paper.
That way you can glance down occasionally using it as a roadmap.
There's a certain particular number that's really important or big concept you want to stress.
It's right there on your single sheet of paper, but it's not a big stack of papers where people are
expecting five minutes and they see this and their first reaction, Oh my gosh, this person's going

Now you need your notes on a single sheet of paper, which, by the way, that's what great speakers

--- Public Speaking Rules You Should Never Break Public Speaking ---

What are some of the top rules you should never break when giving a speech or presentation?
One rule never read a speech.
The hardest thing you could ever do is read a speech without completely boring people to death.
Unless you are a trained actor and a really good trained actor, if you try to read a speech, it destroys
your eye contact.
It makes your voice flat, boring, monotone, and too consistent in speed and pitch and volume.
So whatever you do, don't try to read a speech.
The next thing, don't try to read PowerPoint slides.
Turning your back to the audience.
They can see the back of your head and you're reading a bunch of slide.
Horrible thing to do.
People hate it and they're simply going to ignore you.
Next thing, don't ever apologize for your speech.
Oh, I'm sorry.
I wish I had more time to prepare.
I'm sorry I didn't have the right stuff.
Don't apologize about your speech.
Simply give the best speech you can.
Next.
Don't go on too long.
Now, it's not true that you have to speak three minutes or that shorter is always better.
But if you're budgeted a half an hour and you're still talking at 50 minutes, that's a big problem
for everybody, even if you have interesting content.
So don't violate the amount of time you have allocated for your presentation.
The final thing is don't just do a data dump.
Don't try to cram as many facts and figures and numbers into your speech because you are guaranteed
not to communicate.
People are going to tune you out.
They will not remember anything.
So there are a lot of do's and don'ts you can avoid and still be successful.
But you've got to avoid the biggest blunders common in many, many speaking disasters.

--- How Long Should My Speech Be Public Speaking ---

How long should my speech be and how can I be more concise?
Let me stop you right there.
Your goal shouldn't ever be to be concise.
Your goal should be communicating ideas that are important to you, interesting and relevant to your
audience, and doing so in a way that's actually memorable.
That should be the goal.
So take as much time as you need for that.
Now, there was a study done in 1974 by the US Defense Department that said the perfect length of a
speech was 17.5 minutes.
Personally, I find that complete, utter baloney because we've all seen people who speak for two minutes
and everyone's asleep.
On the other hand, I've seen speakers talk from ten in the morning till midnight.
The audience wanted more.
Why?
Because they were consistently interesting.
So I would be careful about trying to pigeonhole your speech into a specific time amount.
Now, there may be times when you're told you have exactly 20 minutes, you're at a financial conference,
you're told you have exactly 25 minutes and five minutes for Q and A, and you've got to stick to it.
But there are plenty of times in real life where you're talking to your own employees, colleagues and
new business pitch people may have traveled to come see you set up a meeting and it took them an hour
to get there and an hour to get back.
They're going to listen to you.
They're not sitting there with a stopwatch for three minutes.
And the most important thing is that you actually communicate your ideas in an interesting way.
So remember, the choice isn't between being really, really boring for a long period of time versus
really boring for two minutes, if that's the only choice.
Yeah, better to be boring for two minutes.
But there is another option and that is to be incredibly interesting.
Memorable for the amount of time you need to convey your ideas.
So rather than worry about being concise or speaking just for five minutes, focus your on your ideas.
Make sure they're interesting and memorable.
The time will often take care of itself.

--- Tell ’em what I’m gonna tell ’em, tell ’em, Public Speaking ---

They guessed differently.
Here's my point.

You can tell them.
You can tell them what you told them.

Tell them one time in a compelling way.

Tell them three times in a speech and it's boring and they won't remember it three seconds later.

--- How to Prepare a Speech Public Speaking ---

How to prepare a speech.
In a nutshell, do the following.
Brainstorm on every message you could say to this audience on the topic at hand.
Narrow it down to the top five.
Brainstorm on a story or two and an example for each message point.
Come up with a fact or a number for each message point.
Then have a simple one page outline that has no more than 3 or 4 words per line.
Then practice the speech on video.
It can be your own cell phone.
Keep practicing until you like it.
If you do that, you will be ahead of 95% of the public speakers in the world.

--- How to Pace a Speech Public Speaking ---

So how do you pace a speech or a presentation?
The biggest problem most people have is they get a little nervous.
They start speaking too quickly.
And when you speak too quickly, it tends to flatten out your voice.
It essentially destroys the punctuation of speaking.
If you're reading a book, you have certain cues to your eye.
A comma means a pause, a period, a longer pause, a paragraph break, a longer pause, an actual chapter
and a white sheet of paper in between is an even longer break.
But when you're speaking, if everything sort of comes out.
Here's my next data point.
It's like reading one big run on sentence with no punctuation.
You could do it, but it's a lot of work.
So you need to put in pauses.
You need to catch your breath.
Sometimes you can do this by walking a few feet, not saying anything.
You need to look at audience members and see are you getting it?
Sometimes toss out a question to the audience.
Actually have them answer it.
Sometimes you toss out a question and it's simply a rhetorical question and you let people think about
what you said.
You need pausing throughout your speech and you need variation in speed and tone.
Sameness is what kills a speech.
Consistency is what kills a speech.
People think, Oh, I'm being very professional.
Everything's even keeled.
No, you don't want to be even keeled.
You want to be conversational.
That means sometimes faster, sometimes slower, sometimes louder, sometimes softer.
And sometimes a pause is what's most effective.
That's how you pace your speech.

--- How to Put Your Audience at Ease Public Speaking ---

--- How to Give a Formal Speech Public Speaking ---

Should I make my speech, a formal presentation or an informal presentation?
Folks, I'm here to tell you there is no such thing as a formal presentation or an informal presentation
or a PowerPoint presentation or a financial presentation.
There are only two types of presentations in the entire world.
Do you know what they are?
That's right.
It's either good or it's bad from the audience's perspective.
The only thing they're ever thinking is, Wow, this TJ, he's really boring.
I'm not really going to pay attention.
Let me check my email or James over here.
He's interesting.
Let me pay attention.
This is useful.
That's the only thing going on in your audience's mind.
So great speakers adopt the mindset of their audience, not the mindset of the speaker.
You've got to put yourself metaphorically in the chairs of your audience so you can experience this
as they do.
So here's the big problem.
When I hear someone ask about formal versus informal, once somebody tells themselves, Oh, I'm now
giving a formal speech, they tend to make their speech awful.

--- What to Do if You Don't Like Your Voice Public Speaking ---

So what do you do if you simply do not like the sound of your own voice?

Your voice isn't that bad.
Here's my experience, and I've worked with more than 10,000 clients from six continents for the last
30 years.
Most people don't like the sound of their own voice.
Here's why.
When you're hearing your voice come back to you through a speaker because you're watching a video of

distorted way compared to how you normally hear your voice.
You normally hear your voice distorted through the bones in your skull and in your nasal cavities in
your mouth.
So you're hearing your voice all day long in a very distorted way.
So when you hear your voice coming through speakers, yeah, there's still some distortion, but it's
actually much closer to how you sound in real life to everyone else.
So it's not that your voice is bad or awful, it's just that you're not used to hearing your voice and
it's jarring.
Imagine if you are used to looking at yourself in the mirror and you always see one face and now you
see somebody on video, that's you.
And it's a completely different face.
Might not be an ugly face.
It's just weird.
That's kind of what it's like.
There are basically three types of voices in the world, and I'm making these statistics up generally
to make a point.

of the room or jump out the window.
Everybody else, far in excess of 99%, have voices that are just voices.
Not so great.
People are going to pay a bunch of money, not so awful that it drives people away.
My voice is in that category now.
Some people like my voice, some don't.
No one's willing to pay me a ton of money just for my voice.
And no one wants to run out of the room simply hearing me say something.
They might not like what I say, but it's not the tone of my voice.
Chances are you are exactly like that, that your voice simply isn't as bad as you think.
Now, if you truly have some kind of a lisp, a speech impediment, you may want to see a speech therapist.
If you have a nasal problem where your nasal cavities are clogged and that's causing certain problems
and giving you a nasal twang, yeah, maybe you need surgery, but if I were you, I would be far more
interested in actually having something interesting to say when you speak, because that's a problem
we can solve.
I mean, let's say your voice isn't great if you have something truly interesting and memorable to say

Barbara Walters doesn't have a great voice.

--- How Many Slides to Put in a PowerPoint Presentation Public Speaking ---

So how many slides should you put on a PowerPoint presentation?
I know some of you want a very firm answer, like 7 or 10.
It's really not that simple.
Here's the bigger test I would give you.
For each slide you have, ask yourself, Does this slide make my idea more memorable than me simply
saying it?
And does this slide make my idea more understandable than simply saying it?
If you can't get a yes answer to both of those things, you should probably throw the slide away.
Now, having said that, I've seen people who only have 2 or 3 slides in a presentation, and the presentation
was awful because there was nothing interesting or memorable in the slides.
Nothing that enhanced it at all.
I've also seen speakers, well known sales expert Jeffrey Gitomer, for example.
I've seen him give a presentation with 120 slides and it was a great presentation.
Now, it wasn't necessarily great because of the slides, but the slides didn't bring him down.
Your focus should not be the number of slides.
Your focus should be what are the ideas you have to communicate to this audience now?
How can you use every tool possible to make these ideas more understandable, more memorable?
One tool is by telling a story.
Another tool giving an example.
Another tool.
A handout before or after the presentation.
Another tool is a visual that you display and a PowerPoint slide.
Another tool could be a prop.
So focus on what the real goal is.
Communicating your ideas.
Then use all the tools available.
If you do that, the number of slides will take care of themselves.

--- PowerPoint Presentations Require 2 Separate PowerPoints Public Speaking ---

Every PowerPoint presentation should really have two presentations, not just one.
What do I mean by that?
If you're giving a PowerPoint presentation, you really, in my opinion, need to have two separate,
distinct presentations.
There is the PowerPoint that you actually project could be on a small screen.
It could be on a 100 foot screen in front of people.
When you are standing speaking to them, that PowerPoint presentation should be devoid of words, text
complexity columns and complex graphs.
Instead, it should have images.
Pictures.
If there's a graph, it should show one relationship, two variables at most.
There is a second PowerPoint presentation that you also need and that is something that you email to
people in advance or you hand out.
This PowerPoint can have lots and lots of text, lots of data, complexity, wildly complex graphs,
because people can read it, they can print it out, they can twist it, turn it, they can start to
read it, get hungry, put it down, go get a ham sandwich, come back and read it and study it again.
It's a different medium.
The text medium that you control is simply different from a live presentation where the audience can't
control the slides going.
By now, Microsoft PowerPoint has a notes section where you can put notes in it, lots of data.
It shows up to anyone you email the PowerPoint to.
It shows up on any computer screen, but when you're projecting it, it doesn't show up.
So you can actually have two presentations in one file, or you can have it as two completely different
ones.
If you try to have one PowerPoint that has multi purposes, you are going to fail.
I understand that's how most people do it, but I'm here to tell you it is not effective.

--- How to Test Your PowerPoint Slides for Effectiveness Public Speaking ---

How can you test your PowerPoint presentation to see if it's effective or not?
It's actually very easy to test PowerPoint slides to see which ones work and which ones don't.
And it's not about some general axiom like it must be seven points or no more than three.
That's not it.
It's about your audience.
Do they understand it?
Do they remember it?
So here's my advice.
You're giving a big PowerPoint presentation on Friday to 30 clients.
Find three colleagues from down the hall on Wednesday.
Give them your PowerPoint presentation.
When you're done, ask them every slide they remember.
If they don't remember one of your slides, take that slide, tear it up and throw it in the trash can.
You now have empirical evidence that that slide doesn't work?
Again, the goal of your slide is to make your idea more understandable and more memorable.
If your audience can't remember it two seconds after you gave the speech, it obviously isn't effective.
Use this rule and I guarantee you it's going to eliminate your bad slides.
It's also going to eliminate slides with text and bullet points because people never remember those.

--- Should I read my speech so that I don’t make any mistakes Public Speaking ---

Should I read my speech to make sure I don't make any mistakes?
Well, if you ask any presentation coach, this is probably the question we get that drives us bonkers
the most.
It's virtually impossible to read a speech without, by definition, making a mistake.
You've destroyed all eye contact with the audience.
You've become boring, bland, most likely monotone.
Now, it is true there are some people good at reading speech.
Ronald Reagan was good at reading his speech.
I've seen Dan Rather read his speech well, but guess what?
He was reading teleprompter copy and reading scripts every day for 60 years.
If you're reading scripts every day for 60 years, yeah, you'll probably get good at it.
But for most people, business people, people in public life, political life, it's really not a good
idea to read a speech because it instantly handcuffs you, destroys your eye contact, robs you of natural
rhythm in your voice.
Makes you sound phony, contrived, and it just evens out the tones, the volumes, the speed, the
pitch.
It makes things too consistent, and that's boring.
So you may think it's safe to read because that way you won't forget something.
But if you destroy people's ability to pay attention because they've fallen asleep, it's actually not
safe at all.
Reading his speech, in my view, is actually the riskiest thing you could ever do if your goal is to
actually communicate.

B, they're trying to understand.

D By definition, whatever you say next in answer to their question is going to be interesting to that

--- Culture is Everything ---

When you are preparing your presentation for foreign audiences, it's critically important that you
avoid certain cultural references that just aren't going to make any sense to that foreign audience.
Now, the classic example is the American talking about the touchdown and all these football metaphors
and crush them and the huddle and nobody else in the rest of the world knows what they're talking about
because football to the rest of the world means soccer to Americans.
So avoid cultural references that deal with sports specific to you.
That's the biggest blunder.
I find this problem most acute for American businessmen because so many of them do like football and
they make references, you know, blocking and tackling.
All these analogies and references come from football.
So if you're saying it to a foreign audience, they're not going to know what you're talking about and
you're going to lose them.
And you know what happens when a foreign audience is lost by your speech?
Exactly the same thing that happens when a US audience gets lost by your speech.
They tune out and they read their email and you have wasted your time.
So you've got to treat this some respect like any other speech.
You've got to be focused on their audience.
You've got to make sure.
Are they paying attention?
Do they look like they're understanding?
So part of what you've got to do is not completely strip out everything interesting from your speech,
but you've got to make sure your examples, your case studies are things that resonate with people either
everywhere or specific to the country you are in now.
The more advanced you can do with your preparation and research specific to that country, If you can
reference particular sports stars from that country, famous in that country, great.
If you don't have time to do that or you're not willing to do that, make sure your references, your
analogies, your metaphors resonate at the human level.
Everywhere you can talk about family, you can talk about joys, you can talk about childbirth, you
can talk about all sorts of things that translate across culture.
But don't talk about your college football game and things that are really unique to right here in the
US.

--- How to Handle a Heckler Public Speaking ---

So how do you handle a heckler if you're giving a presentation?
Folks.

You don't have to do that, but you do need to make sure that you don't wilt, that you don't act upset,

That's really the most important thing.
And showing patience, don't getting angry, don't elevate the situation.
There may be times when you have to say, look, one of us can speak if it's going to be you, be my

Now, that's not my first choice, but if someone persists or you can take a vote, how many of us want

Or you could just say, Sir, thank you for sharing and then just keep on.
Now I say, sir, because in my experience, most hecklers are men, but there's no one perfect response.
The main thing is don't look bothered, don't run off the stage, don't get flustered, and people will
give you points and credit for handling the situation with class.

--- It Sounds Silly, But this One Tip Helps Massively ---

There's the classic image of the ugly American in a foreign country who's upset that everybody in this
country, whether it's Italy or whether it is Malaysia, doesn't speak English.
Now, it's inexcusable for Americans to be like that, but it is true now when you see something like
that in a movie or a TV show.
There's the classic, I am now talking to you loudly and slowly so you will understand my language.
Obviously, that doesn't work if the person you're speaking to doesn't speak your language.
Now, here's the part that's a little bit confusing or contradictory.
I actually do recommend that when you are speaking to foreign audiences, that you speak a little louder
than normal and a little slower than normal.
Now, hey, we all have cultural biases.
I have a bias.
I'm an American.
I only speak English.
But what I have found in speaking all over the world is there's a tremendous number of people who,
even if English is not their first language, they have a working understanding of English because they've
seen so many movies from Hollywood TV shows in English, they have learned a lot of English.
So here's where speaking a little bit slower helps.
It's simply easier for people to process what you're saying.
When it's slower, they can see the separation between words.
It's easy to sort of hear it, figure it out in their mind.
What is that word that they remembered studying in English class five years ago?
And then they have to translate it from the English word to the word in their language.
That takes time.
Now, I'm not suggesting that you speak like this in a robotic way, because that's annoying.
That's really annoying.
I'm not suggesting that.
But what I am suggesting is speak a little bit slower than normal.
Don't be afraid to pause a little more between sentences, thoughts, paragraphs.
Feel free to walk a little more.
Pause.
Reflect.
Look at people's eyes to see that there is some connection going on.
So it's a subtle thing, but I do recommend speaking a little bit slower than normal longer pauses.
It's going to be much easier for the people in the audience who are translating in their own brain.
But it's also going to make life much easier for the translator because professional translators are
doing an awful lot.
But it's still tough to be speaking out to the audience at the same time having to listen to you.
So when you pause occasionally, they can then say what you just did in the other language, and yet
they haven't missed anything from what you're saying.
So that's the beauty of pausing and also just speaking a little louder than normal is going to make
it easier for anyone to comprehend it.
Again, you're not yelling.
You're not shouting.
You're not the so-called ugly American.
But a little louder, more pausing, will make it much, much easier for everyone to understand and
translate in their own brains.
And that's going to make it more effective for your speech and your presentation.

Sometimes you may have to decide to really engage your audience.

Sally.
I feel like I'm losing some of you.
Tell me, where have I gotten Fuzzy?
Here.
Can you help me out and put the spotlight on someone there?
And maybe someone in the audience can help you out.
But if you just ignore it, you're only going to make the problem worse.
So either change the room, change the temperature, change your subject area, change your direction,
change the style, do something to get yourself out of this rut.

--- Creating Your Permanent Reminders for the Audience ---

I understand finding great translators can be difficult, time consuming, sometimes expensive.

Certainly the title, your key points, if you have other information for them, if they can reach out

So have some kind of handout that's translated in their language of your core content and that will
help your audience.

--- How to Keep Your Speech from Being Boring Public Speaking ---

So how do you keep your speech from being boring?
Because let's face it, the vast majority of presentations in the world are deadly dull and they're
boring.
Now, I hear my clients say that all the time, and yet they stand up and they give boring speeches.
Why is that?
It's because we feel like a speech is really about telling people everything we know, every fact,
every bullet point, every number on a particular subject that has occurred in the last quarter or the
last year.
If that is your assumption going into a speech, you are by definition going to be a failure.
That's not what a speech is about.
If you want to be an effective speaker, if you want to not be boring, you have to use editorial judgment.
You have to look at all the things you could say and figure out what are truly the handful of most important
ideas important to me, but also important to this audience.
And now, how can I flesh it out?
How can I make it more memorable?
How can I give examples?
And most important, how can I tell stories to make these ideas come alive?
If you do that, you will not be boring if you let somebody just start piecing together bullet points
on a PowerPoint slide deck for you, you are going to be boring.

--- Working the Room ---

You finish the speech, you received a polite applause.
Now what?
Well, it's not over my recommendation.
Don't rush out of the room.
Don't try to hop the first plane out of there.
Don't leave the conference to go relax by the pool.
As much as that might be an attraction for you.
Instead, work the room.
Now, you might not be a politician, but you do want to communicate your ideas.
So stay in the room because people may want to ask you questions.
They may have been too intimidated to ask a question in their language or to try to ask in English in
front of people.
But they may be perfectly comfortable talking to you one on one.
And that may be the moment where you really connect with people.
You've answered their question and sometimes you can say, Ah, now I get it.
It also just creates a much stronger personal bond.
People will trust you more, they'll like you more, they'll give you higher evaluations.
If that's relevant to where you are speaking.
So stay in the room, meet as many people as possible, shake hands, be friendly, ask them questions,
and let them ask you questions, because this is still an opportunity for you to communicate.
You're still in the spotlight for that particular room.
You're the biggest celebrity there, so you might as well enjoy your celebrity status while it last.
So talk to people in the room.
Be the last person out of the room and you'll make the most out of this speaking engagement.

--- How to Recover from a Memory Lapse during a Speech Public Speaking ---

So how do you recover from a memory loss during a speech or presentation?
Happens to everyone.
Doesn't matter how old you are or any other factor.
You're giving a presentation, speech, a talk, and all of a sudden you forget what you're going to
say.
Happens to everyone.
Professional speaker, amateur alike.
Here's the difference, though.
Average speakers, mediocre speakers, when they forget what they're going to say, their face instantly
reveals it.
Oh crap.
Or they actually articulate, Oh, I forgot what I'm going to say.
They put a spotlight.
They magnify their words, their mistakes.
And that in and of itself is a mistake.
Great speakers also forget what they're going to say from time to time.
You know what they do.
They'll stop.
Look at you like I just said something so brilliant.
You need a couple of seconds to think about it, or they'll stop, look down, walk a few feet, as
if they're being completely reflective.
Self-assured inwardly.
They're thinking, Uh oh, what am I going to say?
What am I going to say?
Oh, outwardly they're projecting complete calm and the state of being relaxed.
The other thing great speakers understand is the audience can't read my mind.
The audience doesn't know if I forgot something or what's next on my agenda or my outline.
So if I forget it and I come back to it later and cover it, it's still all going to be good, They
won't know.
So realize you don't have to panic.
Your audience doesn't know that you forgot what you're going to say.
So relax.
Take a breath.
Just pause.
It may seem like forever for you, but if it's only two seconds, your audience won't notice it.
They'll actually appreciate it.
Gives them a second to think and reflect upon what you just said.
So it's not crucial to have a perfect memory.
What is crucial is to figure out how to hide it from your audience and not take out a big sign telling
them when you've screwed up.

--- How to Recover from Making a Mistake in a Speech Public Speaking ---

So how do you recover from a mistake or blunder when you're giving a presentation?
Look, everybody makes mistakes from time to time.
I make mistakes.
Here's the difference, though, between how amateurs handle it and real pros.
What most people do, if they make a mistake and they realize it, all of a sudden it's.
They visibly show all their frustration on their face.
They may apologize.
And unfortunately, what happens, even if people can relate to you, it becomes the most memorable
moment of your presentation.
People are feeling sorry for you.
They're feeling sympathy for you.
That's not the emotion you want from your audience.
You want them focused on the ideas you have and why they need to do what you're asking them to do.
So my advice is, if you make a mistake, first of all, you've got to make a judgment.
How big of a mistake is it?
Because there's plenty of mistakes where you didn't say it exactly the way you wanted to, but it's
not factually incorrect.
It's not legally a problem.
It's just not the best way of saying it.
In that case, ignore it or explain it again without referencing your previous mistake.
Now, occasionally you can make a mistake that is a genuine problem.
If you say your profits are up $1 billion last quarter and you meant to say it's $1 million, well you
better correct that right away.
Or the Securities and Exchange Commission could be all over you and you could find yourself in prison.
So in that particular case, I would just state let me correct that.
It's $1 million last quarter, not the first number.
I said state it state in a straightforward way.
Don't apologize, don't look and act like you are holding yourself in contempt.
Just simply go on correct the record in a straightforward way and continue.
Don't let it act like it's bothering you.
You do that and people will not remember your mistakes.
They'll remember your main messages.

--- Build Confidence Through Notes ---

So speaking up at a meeting is different from giving a speech, giving a prepared presentation, giving

--- Make the Right Risk Assessment ---

You may have heard the old expression, there's no such thing as a dumb question or a bad question.
Technically speaking, that's not true.
It is possible to ask a stupid question and have people laugh at you and think you're stupid.
So I'm not going to tell you that there's zero risk in asking questions or speaking up in a meeting.
But you have to weigh that against the other possible negative outcomes from you not saying anything.
Now, it's been my experience that people actually listening to someone ask a question thinking, Oh
my gosh, that's so stupid.
This person is an idiot.
That's relatively rare.
And yet when managers and others are sizing up a group, a team, a bunch of executives and figuring
out who's an executive who really has leadership potential, who's going to rise further and further,
who's going to be the CEO.
People are doing that consciously and unconsciously in every meeting based in part on who's speaking
and who isn't.
And those who never speak out run a very high risk of being perceived as someone not really cut out
for leadership potential, someone who should sort of stay where they are.
Now, folks, that's a real risk.
So when you're weighing risk, you can't simply do it in an unfair way and focus exclusively on the
risk of saying something stupid.
You have to really look at the risk of being seen quiet, uninteresting, unintelligent, nothing to
add, no real insights, no intellectual leadership.
Those are all very real risks you face every single time you don't speak up at a meeting to either add
your insights, give some additional thoughts, or to ask insightful questions.
So please, let's have an honest risk assessment, in my view.
The risk of asking a question that people think is stupid is relatively low.
The risk of staying silent is quite high.

--- How to Give a Sales Presentation Public Speaking ---

How do you give an effective sales presentation?
At some level, every speech is a sales presentation.
You're trying to sell something, you're trying to sell an idea.

But let's say you are trying to sell concrete or a house or any other product or service.

You have to make it tangible.

walking them through how you've already changed people's lives with your product or service.
So sometimes the best way to speak is to let your customers speak for you.
The other thing you've got to do is realize you still have to ask people for their business.
It doesn't matter if you're trying to sell yourself as a candidate, you have to ask for a vote.
If you want someone to buy your mutual fund or anything else at some point.
Again, in a soft sell non-cheesy way, you need to let people know that you would be very happy to
do business with them and ask them for their business.
And I understand plenty of industries, especially financial service industries, are heavily regulated.
Always do what is legally required of you.
Don't do anything that is even close to being a legal gray area.
But to the extent that you can ask people directly for their business in a non pressure, non desperate
way, the better people like to be asked for their business.
And that is quite often the one thing people forget the most in their sales presentations.

--- The Ultimate Confidence Builder ---

When you're speaking in a meeting, you are speaking to a crowd.

And they're making judgments with a lot of different data.

--- How to Give a Motivational Speech Public Speaking ---

How do you give an effective motivational speech?
In a sense, giving a good motivational speech is one of the hardest things you can do because people
feel jaded.
Most people have heard so many motivational speakers over the years, and after a while they all start
to sound the same.
And if they haven't seen them in person, they've seen their infomercials.
The messages that come from most motivational speeches are the same.
Work hard, set your goals, overcome adversity, work every day on something you really believe in.
Pick something you have a passion for.
Associate with people who are already successful doing what?
All of those are perfectly good rules, perfectly good axioms, but frankly don't mean much to people
who've heard them 10 or 1000 times.
So if you want to stand out as an effective motivational speaker, it all comes down to your stories.
You've got to talk about how you personally did this.
You have to reveal things that involve pain for you.
You have to talk about how low you were before you overcame it.
And you have to give people a sense of how what you did is transferable to them.
It can't simply be.
I was having a tough day and I had a hard time with my business and I couldn't raise capital.
But, oh, my daddy's a billionaire.
So I got him to give me a check for $1 million.
That's not motivational.
That just creates envy.
Now, I don't want you and some people are guilty of this.
I don't want you to fabricate your biography and make yourself seem lower or more desperate than you
actually were.
But paint an accurate picture of where you were, what your problem was, how you overcame it, and
then tie it together to how other people can do that as well.
Now, this isn't my own situation, but I do know other public speakers and speaking experts who started
off stuttering in life.
So they went from speaking way, way below average to way above average.
And many prominent speakers in the world Jesse Jackson, Joe Biden, the vice president, spent years
of their lives as stutterers.
So that's highly motivational.
When people hear that they can go to such high levels as speakers knowing they started so far below.
So figure out what your story, what have you truly overcome that motivates people?
If you were born with some rare gift and everything came easily to you might be interesting.
It's not particularly motivational.
People want to know how you overcame something adverse and how they can do the same thing.
What is your secret?
What's your unique twist beyond simply hard work and focus?

--- How to Sound Conversational in a Speech Public Speaking ---

So how do you sound conversational when you're giving a speech?
We've all heard speakers get up and it's sort of like, okay, class, today we're going to cover the
following 12 points and it just sounds awful.
It's this elevated volume, somewhat monotone, and the speaker just sounds like they're reading off
a teleprompter in their brain.
So part of it is you've got to sound like you're actually in the moment that what you're saying and
what you're thinking are in sync.
Because if you're constantly thinking about what you're going to say five seconds from now, it can
make you sound mechanical.
It can make you sound contrived as if you've memorized something, even if you haven't.
Now, this is yet another reason why I recommend not reading a speech, because it's virtually impossible
to sound conversational if you're reading a speech.
It flattens you out.
This is why I recommend speaking from a set outline where you have just bullet points three four words
to remind you of what you want to talk about and then talk about it for a couple of minutes.
Part of it is just getting comfortable.
You need to rehearse, not to memorize, but to get comfortable with your content.
So when you're talking about it, you're not having to think about it.
Think about when someone's asking you, how did you meet your spouse or What's your favorite teacher?
If you're really young.
You don't have to sit there and think about it for ten minutes.
You can just talk.
It's not that you say it word for word the same way every time, but in general, you know what you're
going to say because you've thought about it before and you've said about it.
You've said it before.
That way you can sound conversational.
Also, notice how I just messed up a second ago.
People do that in real life conversation all the time.
It's okay.
Don't beat yourself up.
Don't try to stop and edit it out and iron out all the imperfections.
Realize if you're going to give a speech and you're going to sound conversational, there will be occasional
mess ups.
There will be times when you start a sentence stop and go in another direction.
There will be times when you have sentence fragments.
You'll have repetition.
That's okay.
That's what makes you sound conversational.

The good news about informational speeches is that it's very, very easy to test whether it works or

What information do you take away?
Not whether they like your speech.

You're great, you're charming, you're charismatic, completely irrelevant.

--- Setting the meeting objective -- a critical factor to success ---

What is the purpose of your online meeting?
Sometimes it pays to actually write it down or at least have it crystallized in your brain in one sentence.
The problem with some meetings, whether they're virtual or not, is that they have no purpose.
People are getting together because they feel like, well, we have to have a meeting.
You need to do everything you can to make sure everyone understands what the purpose is of your meeting.
Because if people are confused, it's even easier for people to daydream or get distracted in a virtual
meeting because if the camera's not on them, Twitter, Facebook, blogs.
All right here.
So that is the fundamental starting point for any meeting, whether it's virtual or in person.
What is the clear cut purpose of the meeting and what specific outcome are you looking for?
If you're pitching someone for new business, you're trying to convince them to hire you.
If you are talking to your other managers on a sales strategy, you need buy in on what the strategy
is going to be.
Every single time you meet with someone and speak, you should have some outcome in mind.
Now it may just be to keep them apprised of the work you've been doing in your section for the last
quarter and letting them know that you're doing good work.
But there needs to be something specific and concrete.
Now, if you are a participant in the meeting and it's not yours, try to focus on just one idea you
really want to communicate and what you want people to do with that.
So that is the starting point.
The starting point is not, Oh, what camera should I use?
The starting point is not should I use makeup or not?
The starting point for an online meeting is the same place as any other meeting.
What is it that you hope to accomplish?
Really nail that down first before every meeting.

Video conference meetings, real life meetings.

--- Do NOT Hide Behind Slides - Show Your Face on the Video Meeting ---

Let's address something head on.
If you're a normal person and I assume you are, your first thought might be, well, I don't want to
be on camera.
I'll just speak behind the scenes and I'll put up slides the whole time.
No, no, no, don't do that.
It is so much less interesting to people.
It's boring.
It makes you look cowardly and like you're afraid and you're practically begging people to ignore you
and check email and cell phones and Facebook.
So you don't like the idea of your face on camera?
You want to just use your voice that's easier for you.
You don't want to have to shave or do your hair or clean up.
I've got bad news for you.
Nobody cares what's easy for you.
Your boss, your clients, your customers.
They may like you, but they don't really care about what's easier for you.
Every decision you make has to be looked at through the prism of is this helping the people?
I'm speaking to?
My clients, my customers, my colleagues.
Is it helping them?
And you not showing your face is not helping them.
That is, you just not dealing with fear.
So do not try to just use voice.
All the major applications have systems where you can just call in on phone.
And I know you're tempted to say, Oh, you know, a bad Internet connection today.
I couldn't join us on the video on the website, but I'm here by phone.
You can do that once or twice, but after a while, people will see through that.
So you need to show your face because the face is so much more expressive than the voice alone.
People will capture nuance, figure out what's important.
They will feel much more connected to you and they will listen so much more carefully.
If they can see you now, it's perfectly fine to put up slides for portions of your presentation or
to put up a graph or to share a website.
I'm not suggesting it has to be you the whole time, but if you want people to listen to you and to
really focus on your most important points, you need them to see you so they can see why you think
that is important.
So yes, you do have to show your face if you really want to be seen as competent, confident and professional
for your online meetings.

--- Never Be Nervous Again on Camera ---

In this first big section here, I'm going to start off in a place that most people don't start when
it comes to courses and videos teaching you how to video conference.
Most people start off with a tech side of things.
Well, here's what I know about you.
You're kind of like me in the sense that you're probably more worried about how do you not look stupid?
That's the human response.
So I want to give you solutions to real human needs.
That's what you're going to learn in this section.
All the do's and don'ts of how to really come across comfortable, confident, relaxed, so you don't
have to worry about it if you're nervous about how you look, if you're not confident that you're coming
across your best, none of the other stuff will matter because that will mess up how you communicate.

--- Fundamentals of Effective Online Presentations ---

If you're giving a presentation in an online meeting, realize that many of the things that work in
real life when you're giving presentations also work when you're giving an online presentation.
On the other hand, the things that hurt you in real life will also hurt you if you do the same thing
in an online presentation.
Let's look at the biggest blunders most people make when they are giving speeches, presentations,
talks in real life or online.
The number one blunder is a big data dump.
More and more facts, more and more numbers.
Here's all the charts.
Here's all the graphs, and it's just mind numbingly boring.
Remember, if you're asked to give a presentation, so much of your job is to provide judgment on what
is truly important.
What do the people you're meeting with really need to know in order to take specific actions?
They don't need to know every single thing you know about the subject, otherwise they would have your
job.
So don't drown.
People in data don't show bullet point after bullet point after bullet point and don't stay in the abstract
realm.
You've got to make your ideas come alive.
So let's start at the beginning.
The first thing you need to ask yourself for any presentation is in one sentence What is it I want the
people I'm speaking to to do.
That's the first step.
The next step is then to ask yourself what messages are most likely to motivate them to do what I want
them to do and to narrow it down to just five, just a handful.
I've been teaching people how to speak online and in the real world for more than 30 years.
And I always ask my students the very same question Can you think of the best speaker you've ever seen
in your life?
Now?
Can you tell me how many messages you remember from that speech or that presentation, whether it's
online or in person?
I've never yet had anyone remember more than five ideas from people they heard in their industry.
Sometimes it's zero.
Often it's one or just 2 or 3, but it's never been more than five.
So I believe whether you have a five minute presentation online or a 90 minute presentation, you truly
need to narrow your messages down to just a handful, literally five or fewer.
Next, you need an actual story to bring each message point alive.
Human beings remember stories.
They visualize stories.
They process stories.
Yes, they can understand facts, but facts are quickly forgotten.
When I ask my clients all over the world, what do they remember from the best speaker?
They always say, I remember the story that this woman said, and they go in and tell the details of
the story, even if it's been ten years since they heard it.
People remember stories now important that the stories are relevant to your audience, what they need
to know.
It can't be personal or self-indulgent.
It can be personal if it relates to how you helped other clients, colleagues, customers solve a real
problem, then the personal stories are the absolute best.
If you have extra facts or figures, have them on a sheet of paper.
Glance down at them.
If you want to put up a particularly powerful image, put it up on the screen for people to look at
or 1 or 2 facts, put it up there for people to look at.
If you have a traditional PowerPoint slide deck, my recommendation email that in advance, offer to
email it to them after the online meeting.
But don't just be going through a deck quickly fastly while you're talking over a bunch of slides that
just puts everyone to sleep.
Now you need to practice your speech.
Really rehearse it and I say speech, presentation, talk.
I just mean your mouth is moving.
You're trying to communicate ideas, in this case online.
You need to practice it on video until you like it.
And then ideally, if you have a good one on video before your actual live event, send it out to a
few colleagues.
Get feedback from them.
These are the fundamentals that will really carry you a long way when it comes to your online meetings.
So many people make the mistake of fixating on the right camera and the right light and the right microphone
and makeup and all this.
But then they start to speak and it's boring because they're reading or it's just a date.
None of this other stuff matters if you're putting everyone to sleep.
And as you've heard me mention, one of the aspects of online meeting is it's never been easier for
people to literally fall asleep.
They can hit the mute button.
The camera isn't on them, and we don't want to make it easier for them to do that.
So these are the fundamentals of the presentation.
You still need to speak in a way that's interesting, understandable and memorable.
If you do that online or offline, you'll be in great shape.

The future of storytelling is not about choosing between AI and human creativity, but about how we

--- Top 5 Storytelling Techniques for Making Virtual Presentations Feel Personal ---

In today's digital age, making virtual presentations feel personal is more crucial than ever.
With the shift towards remote work and online meetings, capturing and maintaining your audience's attention
through a screen presents unique challenges.
However, with the right storytelling techniques, you can bridge the virtual gap and create a compelling,
engaging experience for your listeners.
Let's dive into the top five storytelling techniques that can transform your virtual presentations.
Firstly, personal stories are your secret weapon.
Sharing personal experiences not only humanizes you to your audience, but also makes your content relatable.
When you open up about your challenges, successes, or lessons learned, you create an emotional connection.
This connection is the foundation of engagement, making your audience more invested in what you have
to say next.
Secondly, the power of visuals cannot be overstated.
In a virtual setting, your audience's attention can easily wander.
By incorporating relevant, captivating visuals into your presentation, you grab their attention and
help them visualize your message, whether it's through infographics, videos, or powerful images.
Visuals serve as anchors, keeping your audience focused and engaged.
Thirdly, interactive elements play a crucial role in making virtual presentations feel personal.
Polls, Q&amp;A sessions, and interactive quizzes break the monotony and foster a sense of participation.
These elements not only keep your audience on their toes, but also provide valuable feedback, allowing
you to tailor your presentation in real time to better meet their needs and interests.
Fourthly, storytelling is not just about what you say, but how you say it.
Vocal variety and pacing are essential tools in your storytelling arsenal.
By varying your tone, speed, and volume, you create dynamics in your presentation that can emphasize
key points, build suspense, or convey emotions.
This vocal engagement keeps your audience hooked as they're constantly anticipating what comes next.
Lastly, the use of metaphors and analogies can make complex ideas more accessible and memorable.
By drawing parallels to familiar concepts, you simplify the information, making it easier for your
audience to understand and retain metaphors and analogies not only aid comprehension, but also add
a creative flair to your presentation, making it more enjoyable and impactful.
In conclusion, virtual presentations present unique challenges in connecting with your audience.
However, by incorporating personal stories, leveraging powerful visuals, engaging your audience interactively,
utilizing vocal variety, and simplifying complex ideas with metaphors and analogies, you can make
your virtual presentations feel as personal and impactful as face to face meetings.
These storytelling techniques are not just strategies, but essential tools for effective communication
in the digital era, enabling you to captivate and influence your audience from anywhere in the world.

--- Case Study: How Netflix and Spotify Use Personalization to Drive Engagement ---
